en: The King said:
O sage, how did Priyavrata, who was devoted to the Lord and delighted in the Self, take pleasure in household life— that very root which is the bondage of karma and the cause of downfall?

O best of the twice-born, such an attachment to household life as this could surely not belong to those great souls who are free from all attachments and whose minds are fixed on the feet of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka). O brahminical sage, it is impossible for such men to remain attached to their homes.

For those whose minds are cooled by the shade [of his feet], there is no longing for family life; O Brahman, this is a great paradox: that while he was attached to wife, home, children, and so forth, he attained perfection and his mind became unwaveringly fixed on Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Śuka said:

"Truly, O Blessed One, you have spoken well. My mind is steeped in the nectar of the honey from the glorious lotus feet of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka). Yet, this most auspicious discourse, beloved by the paramahaṃsa devotees, has been somewhat interrupted by obstacles."
O King,

when that prince Priyavrata— a supreme devotee of the Lord who had directly realized the true nature of the ultimate reality through his service at the feet of Nārada— was about to be initiated into the Brahma-satra sacrifice, he did not generally urge others toward that same path.
Having been invited by his father to protect the surface of the earth, because he was the sole vessel for the multitude of preeminent virtues prescribed [for such a task],
he— having through the yoga of uninterrupted meditative absorption merged the entire complex of causal factors and actions into the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself—
did not at all welcome that [invitation], even though it was not to be rejected, since there was no one else besides himself who could occupy that office.
Even so, observing the impending downfall [of the world],
the Blessed One, the primordial God, whose intention for the entire universe was resolved through meditation upon the expansion of this creation of the modes (*guṇa*),
who is self-born and surrounded by his own retinue of all the Vedas, descended from his own abode.

There, like the lord of stars in the expanse of the sky, he was honored along the way by the hosts of immortals with rows of celestial chariots; and being celebrated at every step by throngs of Siddhas, Gandharvas, Sādhyas, Cāraṇas, and Munis in their respective groups,
he approached, illuminating the valley of Gandhamādana.
There, the celestial sage (Nārada), perceiving his father, the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, arriving by means of a swan-drawn vehicle, suddenly rose and, along with his father and son,
stood before him with palms joined in reverence and offered worship.

O descendant of Bharata, the Blessed One— the Original Person, whose multitude of virtues and incarnations are exceedingly praised by hymns— having accepted the worship thus presented, looked upon Priyavrata with a compassionate smile.
Thus he spoke;
the Blessed Lord said:
"Understand this, my son, for I speak the truth: you ought not to feel resentment toward the immeasurable God."
"O Bhava, we are your sons, O Father; we are all great sages who carry out the destiny of this one against our will.
No embodied being can, by means of austerity, knowledge, the power of yoga, intelligence, wealth, or virtue—whether derived from another or from oneself—overcome that which has been ordained."

O dear one, for the sake of existence and destruction, for performing action, and for constant sorrow, delusion, and fear—for pleasure and pain—the people assume a connection with a body ordained by the Unmanifest.
Just as we are firmly bound by the cords of our qualities and actions upon the string of speech, which is so difficult to cross, O child; [so too are they bound to this body].

We all offer tribute to the Lord, like two-legged and four-legged creatures bound by a cord. Indeed, my dear, we receive whatever suffering or happiness is sent forth by the Lord due to attachment to the qualities and their actions; we follow each thing He has assigned us, like the blind being led by those with sight.
Even though liberated, one should maintain one's own body as long as the momentum of past actions (*ārabdha*) remains, experiencing its fruits while free from egoistic identification (*abhimāna*).
Just as one returns from sleep to experience what was previously perceived, the liberated soul does not, however, draw in the *guṇas* for the sake of another body.
For fear may still arise even in the forests for one who is heedless, since he continues to dwell with the six internal enemies.
What fault can the householder’s life bring to the wise man who has conquered his senses and finds delight in the Self?

He who, desiring to conquer the six enemies, first enters the home and strives [therein], transcends even powerful foes by relying on that fortress; once they are weakened, the discerning man may wander at will.
"But you, O lotus-navelled one, having taken refuge in the fortress of the sheath of Your lotus feet, having conquered the six enemies,
and being free from attachment, enjoy here the pleasures bestowed by the Supreme Person, while remaining devoted to Your own nature.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed, the great devotee, with his neck bowed in humility before the command of the Lord, the teacher of the three worlds, replied "So be it" with great respect.

The Blessed One, having been duly honored by Manu, departed while observing Priyavrata and Nārada with impartiality, proceeding toward that state which is equal to the Self, beyond the reach of speech and mind, and unconditioned by worldly activity.

Manu also, his desires thus fulfilled by the Supreme, having installed his son for the protection and preservation of the entire circle of the earth with the approval of the best of the celestial sages, himself desisted from the hope for that pool of water which is the extremely treacherous poison of sense-objects.
Thus indeed did that lord of the world, whose authority over karma was established by the will of the Lord, [attain liberation].

By the power of incessant meditation upon the pair of feet of the Blessed One, the Primordial Person, whose majesty is intent on destroying the bonds of the entire world, his heart’s impurities were thoroughly scorched; though he was already purified, he increased the pride of the great as he ruled the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, he married the daughter of the Prajāpati Viśvakarman, named Barhiṣmatī.
In her, he indeed begot ten sons who were noble in their self-nature, possessing qualities, actions, forms, and vigor equal to his own,
and a youngest daughter named Ūrjasvatī;
[the sons were] Āgnīdhra, Idhmajihva, Yajñabāhu, Mahāvīra, Hiraṇyaretas, Ghṛtapṛṣṭha, Savana, Medhātithi, Vītihotra, and Kavi— all of whom bore the names of fire.

Among these, there were three—Kavi, Mahāvīra, and Savana—who were perpetual celibates (*ūrdhva-retas*). Having cultivated proficiency in the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-vidyā*) from their very childhood, they entered exclusively the order of the paramahaṃsas.
Indeed, in that state, those supreme sages of tranquil character [meditated] upon the abode of the entire multitude of living beings...

Through the power of uninterrupted remembrance of the glorious lotus feet of the Blessed Vāsudeva, who is the refuge of the frightened, their inner hearts were permeated by the flow of supreme devotional yoga; thus, having realized the Lord— who is the Self of all beings and the indwelling Self—
they attained identity with Him, the Self, without distinction.
By another wife he had three sons— Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata— who were the presiding lords of successive Manvantaras.

Thus, while his own sons were established in the ways of tranquility, the Lord of the Earth [Pṛthu] for eleven billion years oppressed the earth with the twanging of the bowstring on his pair of staff-like arms, which were filled with the essence of unimpeded human prowess, thereby quelling all adversaries of Dharma.

In Barhiṣmatī, the high-minded king enjoyed himself daily, as if his discernment were overcome and he were unaware of anything else by the playful glances, charming laughter, and other gestures of the women, whose joy was ever-increasing and who were possessed of a youthful passion that eclipsed their modesty.
This continued for as long as the divine sun, circling the mountain of the gods, illuminated the surface of the earth.
With one half he scorched, and with the other half he covered; for at that time, his own power having been augmented by the worship of the Blessed One,
disregarding that [sun], he traversed Vastarāṇi seven times with a swift, light-filled chariot, thinking, "I shall turn even the night into day," like a second sun.

The moats formed by the rims of the wheels of that chariot became the seven oceans; from where they were thus created, the seven islands of the earth arose—namely Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara. Their dimensions increase twofold in succession from each preceding one, and they are arranged all around on the outside.
He gave his daughter named Ūrjasvatī to Uśanas, in whom was born Devayānī, the daughter of Kāvya;
such human effort as this is not possible for men whose six material qualities have been conquered by the dust of the feet of the Wide-striding Lord.
It is wonderful that even one who has gone far away might take up that name but once; by doing so, he immediately abandons his bondage.

Thus, although he possessed immeasurable strength and prowess, at one time, through contact with the flow of qualities descending from the feet of the divine sages, he considered himself as if unsatisfied.
Filled with self-disgust, he said:
"Alas! A wicked deed has been committed, in that I have been made to dwell by the senses in this blind well of treacherous objects fashioned by ignorance.
Enough, enough! Shame, shame on me, who am but a deer for the amusement of this woman! Thus he reproached himself.
Having divided this earth among his sons— who had been instigated by their own self-reflection attained through the grace of other deities—
according to their respective shares, and having abandoned his queen, whose enjoyments were exhausted and who was like a corpse, along with his great royal splendor,
he himself, having conceived detachment within his heart and having taken hold of the majesty of Hari’s pastimes, [followed] the venerable Nārada...
He followed that very same path once again.
Regarding this, there are indeed these verses:
"Who indeed, other than the Lord, could perform the deeds accomplished by Priyavrata?"
He who, by the depressions of his wheel-rims, created shade while destroying the seven oceans;

he by whom the configuration of the earth was established with its rivers, mountains, forests, and so forth; and he by whom boundaries were set in each island according to their divisions for the welfare of living beings.

He who is dear to his younger brothers made even his earthly, celestial, and human greatness—born of the yoga of action—seem like hell; Śrī Śuka said: BhP_05.01.040/1 bhūmaṃ divyaṃ mānuṣaṃ ca mahitvaṃ karma-yogajam / BhP_05.01.040/2 yaś cakre nirayopamyaṃ puruṣānujana-priyaḥ // BhP_05.01.001/0 Śrī Śuka said:

While his father was thus engaged, Āgnīdhra, abiding by his instructions, protected the subjects dwelling in Jambūdvīpa like his own biological children, looking after them with regard for their welfare.

Once, desiring the world of the ancestors, that ascetic, having brought the requisites for service, began to worship the Blessed Lord, the Master of the creators of the universe, in a valley of the mountain where the wives of the best of gods sport, with one-pointed concentration of self.
Perceiving that, the Blessed One, the Primal Person, dispatched an Apsarā named Pūrvacitti, who was singing in the assembly.
She [arrived at] his hermitage grove, which was exceedingly beautiful and variegated with pairs of land-birds perched upon golden creepers entwined among the thick clusters of various trees,
and awakened by the cries of water-fowl, *kukkuṭas*, *kāraṇḍavas*, *kalahaṃsas*, and others, which were resonant with the sounds of the Vedas.
He wandered through the lotus-filled pond whose waters were resonant with the warbling of birds.

Hearing, step by step, the tinkling sound of her beautiful anklets as she moved with the graceful gait and playful movements of her lovely steps, the prince slightly opened his pair of lotus-bud eyes— which had been closed in the yoga of meditation— and looked at her.

Not far from her, she was like a female bee inhaling the fragrance of flowers; with her gait, movements, modesty, humility, glances, beautiful voice, and graceful limbs—which bestowed delight upon the minds and eyes of gods and men—she created an opening in the hearts of men for the flower-armed god of love.

Furthermore, by the obstruction caused by swarms of bees blinded with intoxication at the fragrance of her laughter and sweet speech, which were like nectar flowing from her own mouth, she captivated all.

With his feet moving swiftly, he brought the Goddess—who possessed lovely quivering jar-like breasts, a mass of braided hair, and a girdle—under the sway of the Lord Makaradhvaja, whose opportunity had been revealed by that sight; and, rendered as if senseless, he spoke thus:
"O best of sages, who are you, and what do you intend to do on this mountain? (BhP 5.2.7)
You must be some form of the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Supreme Deity, the Lord;
you carry two bowstrings-less bows for the sake of Your own dear friend. Or else, do You seek out the heedless deer in the forest?

"O Blessed One, we do not know for what purpose you intend to yoke these two arrows of yours— lotus petals that are peaceful, beautiful even without feathers, and possessing exceedingly sharp points— as you wander in the forest."
May Your prowess be for our protection, O Lord of dull intellects;
these disciples of the Blessed One are reciting and constantly singing the Sāman with its secret lore to the Lord on all sides.
All the hosts of sages receive the showers of flowers tossed from your crest like the branches of the Vedas;
[I offer] this speech, like a partridge in the cage of your feet.
O Brahmin, let us hear from you that which is beyond form;
for we have obtained [the vision of] her whose beautiful face is like the crescent of the moon, while where is the circle of firebrands and your bark garment?

"O twice-born one, what has been gathered within these two beautiful horns of yours, between which you carry such a slender body upon which my gaze rests? Is this reddish-brown mud fragrant, and is your own horn like this?"
O fortunate one, by whom you make my hermitage fragrant,
O best of friends, show me that world of yours where such unprecedented limbs as these exist upon the chest.
In the mouth of one like me, who uplifts the mind, there is much wonder—the nectar of the delightful *rāsa* dance and other such things.
O dear one, what personal conduct could there be for one who eats the sacrificial offering? It is only natural.

O Viṣṇu, may your face be like a lake: your unblinking eyes are its two crocodiles; your pair of ears is a pair of agitated fish; the rows of your teeth are its shimmering reeds; and the swarm of bees near you is its lotus.
That moth which was struck by your lotus-hand and is now wandering through the quarters, causes my eyes to tremble as it flutters about;
do you not remember that mass of matted hair released from your face?
"Alas, this wicked wind carries away my lower garment! O ascetic,
whose wealth is austerity, by what austerity have you obtained this form that destroys the penance of those who practice it?"

"O friend, you ought to perform austerities together with me; for what favor does that Lord, the creator of existence, bestow upon me? Yet, I do not abandon you, my beloved, who were granted to me by the gods of the twice-born."
O beautiful-horned one, you ought to lead me, who am devoted to you, to that place where even our mind and sight cannot reach once they have become attached; for from there,
may auspicious attendants come to serve us.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, with a discourse characterized by rustic cleverness, he who was highly skilled in winning over women—possessing the intellect of a wise man—honored that celestial maiden.
And she, in turn, [was captivated] by the intelligence, character, beauty, youth, splendor, and magnanimity of that leader of the host of heroes.
With his mind captivated by him, he enjoyed the pleasures of the earth and heaven for a period of time characterized by tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years as the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Indeed, in her, that best of kings, Āgnīdhra, begot sons known as Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta, Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, Bhadrāśva, and Ketumāla.
She gave birth to nine sons; having borne those nine sons, Pūrvacitti abandoned them at home for a year and once again attended upon the god Aja.

By the grace of their mother, the sons of Āgnīdhra were endowed with innate strength and robust frames; they were divided by their father among the regions of Jambūdvīpa, which were named after himself, according to their respective portions.

The priest Āgnīdhra, never satiated with desires, day after day meditated upon the Apsarā [Merudevī] and, through sacred hymns, attained residence in the same world as she, where the ancestors rejoice.

When his father had passed away, his nine brothers married Merudevī—the daughter of Meru—along with Pratirūpā, Ugradaṃṣṭrī, Latā, Ramyā, Śyāmā, Nārī, Bhadrā, and Devavītī; these were their nine wives.
Śrī Śuka said:
Nābhi, desiring offspring but having no children, with a concentrated mind performed sacrifices to the Blessed Lord, the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), together with Merudevī.
As he was sacrificing with faith and a purified disposition while the Pravargya rites were being performed, [the Lord appeared].
Although the Blessed One is difficult to attain due to the requirements of materials, place, time, mantras, officiating priests, sacrificial fees, and ritual procedures, He—

being well-disposed through His affection for His devotees and having seized their hearts with the desire to fulfill the wishes of His own people— manifested Himself, who is invincible, heart-stealing, and delightful to the mind, eyes, and limbs.
Then, indeed, he beheld that extraordinary golden Person, who had manifested his two pairs of arms;
who wore garments of tawny silk; whose chest was adorned with the shining Śrīvatsa mark; who was distinguished by a forest garland of choice blossoms, the Kaustubha jewel, a mace, and other emblems;
and who was decorated with ornaments for every limb, such as a crown, earrings, bracelets, a waist-string, necklaces, armlets, and anklets, all emitting brilliant rays of light.

The officiating priests, the assembly members, and the householder, like poor men who have suddenly acquired the most excellent wealth, approached him with great reverence, bowing their heads in worship.
The officiating priests said:
"O most worthy one, you ought to accept our repeated offerings; let there be salutation after salutation—this much alone is sufficient."
What man, whose mind is distracted by the qualities of material nature and who is powerless before the Supreme Lord, is capable of defining the form of the Lord— who is well-trained in all things—

by means of the names, forms, and appearances belonging to the realm of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*? Indeed, You are supremely satisfied even by worship offered with water from which the impurities of all classes of people have been removed, and with white sprouts of *tulasī*, *dūrvā* grass, and other offerings, made variegated by the sounds of the affectionate voices of Your attendants, and consisting of a mere fraction of Your most auspicious and excellent multitude of qualities.
Moreover, we do not perceive here any appropriate purpose for you in this sacrifice, which merely bears a heavy burden; for you,

whose very nature is the complete fulfillment of all human goals that manifest directly and without distinction at every moment, this [sacrifice] can only be a means of propitiation for those who pray for blessings from a master.

Just as for the ignorant who do not know their own supreme welfare, You, O Supreme-Person, out of Your most excellent compassion, desiring to bestow upon them Your own majesty known as liberation, did not remain unperceived here like others; rather, You were perceived by Yourself.
Furthermore, this indeed is the greatest boon, O Most Worthy One: that at the sacrifice of the royal sage, You, the bull among givers of boons, became an object of the vision of Your own person.

For those sages who have shaken off all impurities by the fire of sharp, detached knowledge, whose nature is identical to Yours, and who delight in the Self— [for them] the narration of Your multitude of qualities, which are the supreme abode of auspiciousness and are constantly recited as a multitude of virtues,

[is sufficient]. But for us, who are helpless in moments of stumbling, hunger, falling, yawning, or other such distresses, may Your names, formed from Your qualities and which destroy all defilements even in the state of feverish death, somehow serve as a means of remembrance.
May these words come within the range of your speech.

Furthermore, this royal sage, desiring offspring and hoping for a child such as yourself, approaches you—the Lord of all blessings, even of heaven and liberation—with his prayers; for he places his trust in your progeny as one trusts in the Giver of Wealth for riches.
Like one who is destitute of wealth seeking mere chaff,

who here in this world— unconquered by Your unconquerable illusory power (*māyā*), whose path is not yet traversed, whose intellect is unenlightened, whose nature is not shielded from the poison of sense objects, and who has not worshipped the feet of the Great One— could possibly be spared?

O You of abundant deeds, since we have been summoned here with the hope of attaining our goals, yet remain dull-witted, it is only right that You, O God of gods, should forgive our offense against You with equanimity.
Śrī Śuka said: While he was being thus praised with these recitations by those who were ignorant [of his true nature],
the Blessed One— the bull among the immortals, whose feet were saluted and worshipped by the inhabitants of the mountain ranges— spoke these words with compassion.

The Blessed Lord said: O sages, oh! I have been requested by you, whose words are never false, for a boon that is difficult to obtain—namely, that my son should be like me. Indeed, I alone am the most beautiful of all because of my uniqueness; nevertheless, this is a declaration of Brahman.
"It cannot be false, for my own mouth is the assembly of the twice-born and the gods;
therefore, finding no one equal to myself, I shall descend into the Āgnīdhrīya fire by means of a portion of My own self.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus addressed her husband while Merudevī was gazing upon him, the Blessed One vanished.
Śrī Śuka said:
Now, from his very birth, he manifested the characteristics of the Lord through equanimity, tranquility, detachment, sovereignty, and great opulence.
The subjects, the people, the brahmins, and the deities—seeing his majesty increasing day by day—craved him exceedingly as he descended to the surface of the earth.
Indeed, because of his preeminent stature, his vast fame, his vigor, strength, opulence, renown, heroism, and valor, his father gave him this name: "Ṛṣabha.

For Indra, competing with him, did not send rain upon his kingdom; perceiving this, the blessed Lord Ṛṣabhadeva, the master of yoga, laughed and, through the illusory power of his own yoga, [protected] his own realm.
He rained down upon the one named Ajanābha. But Nābhi, having obtained excellent progeny just as he had desired, overwhelmed by a weight of supreme joy,
spoke with a voice faltering from emotion to the Blessed One, the Ancient Person, who had freely assumed the common characteristics of the human world:

With a mind sporting in *māyā*, he attained supreme bliss while affectionately caressing his son, saying, "O child, my dear! King Nābhi, whose affection was known by the citizens, the subjects, and the people of the countryside, consecrated his son for the protection of the boundaries of time and entrusted him to the *brāhmaṇas*; then, together with Merudevī, he entered the city of Viśālā and, through serene and skillful austerity and the yoga of meditative absorption, [attained liberation].
Worshipping the Blessed Vāsudeva, who is known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, he attained his majesty in due time, O son of Pāṇḍu; regarding him, they cite these two verses:
"Who indeed would emulate that deed of the royal sage Nābhi? [...]"
Through his pure deeds, Hari became his offspring;
O Brahmins, how could anyone other than Nābhi be honored as auspicious by the wise,
he who by his power caused the Lord of Sacrifice to appear upon his sacrificial altar?

Then, indeed, the Blessed Lord Ṛṣabhadeva, considering his own realm to be a field for the performance of duty, having demonstrated the life in the teacher’s household and being permitted by his gurus who had granted him boons, while training himself in the duties of householders in Jayantī,
the daughter of Indra, applied himself to the dual form of action prescribed in the traditional scriptures for the sake of his sons.
He begot one hundred sons equal to himself, among whom the great yogi Bharata was the eldest and possessed the most excellent qualities; because of him, this land is designated as Bhārata-varṣa.
Following him were the ninety-nine principal sons: Kuśāvarta, Ilāvarta, Brahmāvarta, Malaya, Ketur, Bhadrasena, Indraspṛk, Vidarbha, and Kīkaṭa.
Kavi, Havis, Antarikṣa, Prabuddha, Pippalāyana,
Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, and Karabhājana—

these nine great devotees were seers of the dharma of the Lord. Their virtuous conduct, which magnified the majesty of the Blessed One and brought about tranquility, was recounted in the dialogue between Vasudeva and Nārada.
We shall describe this further below.

The eighty-one younger sons, known as the Jāyanteyas, were obedient to their father's command; they became Brāhmaṇas who were great householders (*mahā-śālīna*), great Vedic scholars (*mahā-śrotriya*), devoted to sacrifice, and pure in their actions.
The Blessed One, named Ṛṣabha, was self-dependent and, by his very nature, eternally free from the succession of misfortunes.

The Lord himself, who is the experience of absolute bliss, acting as if contrary [to his nature], undertakes actions; by means of his conduct, he teaches through example the dharma that accords with time.
Being impartial toward those ignorant of him, tranquil, friendly, and compassionate, he restrains the world in household life by securing dharma, wealth, fame, progeny, happiness, and immortality.
Whatever conduct the head of a community practices, that very same conduct the world follows.
Although he himself knew the entire dharma—the secret Vedic teaching—he governed the people by means of conciliation and other methods along the path shown by the Brahmins.

Furthermore, he performed sacrifices a hundred times exactly according to the instructions, with all the various rites accumulated through offerings of materials, place, time, age, faith, officiating priests, and diverse purposes.

Protected by the Lord, the Bull among men, in this land no person ever desires anything that does not already exist for him from another source; nor does he look upon anything at any time from anyone other than his own master,
except for the overflowing affection manifested toward him at every moment.

Once, while wandering, the Blessed One Ṛṣabha arrived at Brahmāvarta and, in the assembly of the foremost Brahmanical sages, spoke as follows, even while instructing his sons— who were themselves restrained by the weight of humility and affection— though they were already attentive and listening to him with focused minds.
Ṛṣabha said:

O sons, this body of those who partake of it in the world of men is not fit for the wretched desires of those who feed on excrement; rather, by means of divine austerity, the quality of goodness (*sattva*) is purified, from which arises infinite bliss in Brahman.
They say that service to the great is the door to liberation, while association with those attached to women is the door to darkness.

Those who are impartial, serene, free from anger, and well-wishers are the great and saintly ones; or rather, those who have established their friendship and purpose in Me, the Lord, and not among people who are merely concerned with maintaining the body.
In this world, those who possess wives and children in their homes are not truly filled with joy, nor are they satisfied with mere material objects;
indeed, being heedless, one performs forbidden acts (vikarma) when one strives to gratify the senses.
I do not consider this body to be good, for although it is unreal, it brings suffering to the self.
Defeat arises from a lack of awakening as long as one does not seek to know the reality of the Self;
as long as there are ritual actions, so long indeed does this mind consist of action, by which the bondage of the body persists.
Thus the mind, under the influence of action, employs itself while ignorance is being superimposed upon the Self.

As long as one does not have love for Me, Vāsudeva, one is not released from the bondage of the body. When the wise man, though previously negligent regarding his own true interest, suddenly perceives the improper pursuit of the modes of nature, he loses his memory; like an ignorant man, he finds suffering upon entering a household life based on sexual union.
This union of man and woman is called the mutual knot of their hearts;
from this arises the delusion of people regarding house, field, children, kin, and wealth, in the form of "I" and "mine.
When this firm knot of the mind and heart, bound by karma, becomes loosened...
Then, liberated from this world, a person passes beyond its cause and attains the Supreme,
by means of devotion and constant attendance upon Me— the *haṃsa*, the Guru— through freedom from thirst for sense objects, through endurance of the dualities,
through the realization that all living beings are subject to calamity, through the desire for knowledge, and through the cessation of the impulse toward worldly austerity.

O sons, by means of My activities and discourses on Me, through constant association with My devotees and the chanting of My qualities; through freedom from enmity, equanimity, and tranquility, and through the desire to abandon the notion of "self" regarding the body and home; and through the yoga of the supreme self (*adhyātma-yoga*), service in solitude, and the simultaneous conquest of the vital breaths, the senses, and the ego—[you shall attain Me].
With true faith, through perpetual celibacy, vigilance, and restraint of speech;

with knowledge that perceives my presence everywhere and is adorned by realized wisdom; and through yoga joined with fortitude, effort, and goodness—the skillful one should cast off the subtle body known as the "I-notion."
Being vigilant, one should completely eliminate the accumulation of karma— the knot of the heart acquired through ignorance—

by means of this yoga according to the instructions, and then desist from yoga. A king or a teacher who desires the world of the virtuous should do so for the sake of my grace, [instructing] their sons and disciples.
Thus, free from resentment, one should instruct those who do not know the Truth, but one should not engage those deluded by ritual action in such works.
What purpose could a person gain by leading someone who has lost their sight into a pit?
For the world itself has lost its vision regarding its own ultimate good; it strives for worldly objects out of excessive desire.

For the sake of a mere fragment of pleasure, the fool harbors mutual enmity and does not perceive his own infinite suffering. Who that is wise and himself acquainted with that [truth], seeing him dwelling within the midst of ignorance, would again— out of compassion— employ that one of perverted intellect, who has gone astray, like a blind man?

He who does not deliver one from the approach of death cannot be a guru, nor can he be one's own kinsman; he cannot be a father, nor can she be a mother; he cannot be the deity, nor can he be a husband. This body of mine is difficult to comprehend, for my heart is indeed *sattva*, wherein righteousness (*dharma*) resides.
"Because unrighteousness was placed on my back, the noble ones call me 'Ṛṣabha' (the Bull).

Therefore, you who were born from my heart, all of you should with an untroubled mind serve this Bharata, who is more venerable than yourselves and our own kinsman; for his service is the support of all beings."
Among beings, those superior to plants are the reptiles; among them, the best are those established in consciousness.
From them come humans, then the Pramathas, and even beyond them, the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and those who follow the gods.
Among the gods and Asuras, the foremost are Indra and others, while Dakṣa and his kin are the sons of Brahmā among them.
Bhava is superior, and he is the source of Viriñca’s potency; I am devoted to him, for I am the God of gods among the twice-born.

O brahmins, I do not see any other being equal to the brāhmaṇas; what indeed could be greater than this? Whatever is offered with faith by men, I eat that at will, but not so in the Agnihotra sacrifice.
This ancient, longing body was assumed by Me, by whom there exists here the supreme, purifying essence (*sattva*),
wherein reside tranquility, self-control, truthfulness, compassion, austerity, forbearance, and realization;
and beyond even Me— the Infinite, the Supreme, the Lord of heaven and liberation— there is nothing else.

For those who possess devotion unto Me and are destitute of all else, what need have they for anything other? O sons, you must regard all moving and non-moving beings at every step as My own abode; for those with discerning vision, that indeed is the proper offering to Me.
Indeed, this direct realization of that which is sought by the mind, speech, sight, and the senses is my true provision;
for without it, a person is unable to escape the nooses of Death due to great delusion.
Śrī Śuka said:

Having thus instructed his sons— who were already self-disciplined— for the sake of instructing the world, the high-souled Lord Ṛṣabha, the supreme well-wisher, while training in the *pāramahaṃsya* dharma characterized by devotion, knowledge, and detachment for the great sages of tranquil disposition who had ceased from ritual action, [addressed] the eldest of his hundred sons:
Having consecrated Bharata— a supreme devotee of the Blessed One and one whose sole refuge was the Lord’s people— to protect the earth, he himself,

in that very palace, renounced the world from Brahmāvarta; taking nothing but his body as his possession, like a madman with the sky for his garment and disheveled hair, he established the *āhavanīya* fire within himself and went forth.

Clad in the garb of an ascetic who had renounced all worldly ties—appearing like one who is dull-witted, blind, mute, deaf, a ghost, or insane—he remained silent, having observed a vow of silence even when addressed by people.

Here and there—in cities, villages, mines, hamlets, walled towns, mountain retreats, camps, cowherd settlements, cattle pens, caravans, mountains, forests, hermitages, and along the roads—he was humiliated by the lowest of mortals, just as a forest elephant is harassed by flies; he was subjected to threats, beatings, urination upon him, spitting, the throwing of stones, excrement, and dust, as well as foul odors and harsh words.
Disregarding that very designation of "being" applied to this body— which is characterized by a non-existent configuration and consists of the nature of both [subject and object]—
he wandered alone over the earth with an undisturbed mind, because he remained in his own glory and was free from the superimposed conceits of "I" and "mine.
His limbs, such as his hands, feet, chest, broad arms, shoulders, neck, and face, were arranged with an exquisite and delicate symmetry.

With a face made lovely by a smile whose nature is naturally beautiful, charming with long eyes as cool and reddish as the petals of a fresh lotus, and possessing symmetrical, handsome cheeks, ears, throat, and nose; placing the bow of the flower-arrowed god within the hearts of the city women through the great festival of his face with its concealed smile; and bearing a profuse mass of curly, matted, tawny hair hanging down like pollen.
With his own body soiled by the dust of an ascetic,
he appeared as if possessed by a spirit whenever that Blessed One, as it were, declared this world to be truly contrary to yoga; for,
maintaining the practice of counteracting that [worldly life] by regarding its activities as loathsome, he remained lying down and ate and drank only while in the *ājagara* posture.
Moving about, he would eat, urinate, and belch, leaving the place smeared with his excrement.
The wind carrying the fragrance of his dung made that region ten yojanas all around sweetly scented.
Thus, following the behavior of cows, deer, and crows—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—he acted like a crow, a deer, or a cow, drinking, eating, and urinating.

Thus, the Lord Ṛṣabha— the master of liberation, who practiced various yogic disciplines and experienced uninterrupted supreme great bliss— having fulfilled all his goals through the attainment of yogic powers such as moving through the air, speed equal to the mind, invisibility, entering the bodies of others, and perceiving distant objects, remained with his soul in a state of direct, infinite, and intimate union with the Blessed Vāsudeva, who is the self of all beings.
"O King, he did not welcome with his heart those things that had arrived by chance, rather than directly.
The King said:

"O Blessed One, surely the sovereign powers that arrive by chance cannot again cause suffering for those who delight in the Self, whose seeds of karma have been scorched away by the knowledge impelled by yoga."
The sage said:
"What you have said is true; however, in this world, some do not truly place their trust in the mind, which is as fickle as a deceitful hunter.
And so it has been said:"

One should never form a friendship with one whose mind is unstable, for through trust in such a person, the power of austerity practiced over a long time may be lost. Such a person constantly provides an opening for desire, and enemies follow wherever that opening exists.
For a yogi who has cultivated friendliness, [the Lord] is like a wife to her husband;
yet lust, anger, pride, greed, grief, delusion, fear, and the rest,
as well as the bondage of karma— all of which have Him as their root— what wise man would ever accept them?

Then, although he was the ornament of all the guardians of the worlds, he— whose power as the Lord was unperceived due to his extraordinary dress, speech, and conduct, which were like those of a dullard or a world-renouncer— instructing the yogis in the method for the time of death, desiring to cast off his physical body,
beheld the Self within himself as non-separate and not as a different object; thus, with his worldly activities ceased, he came to rest.

Indeed, the body of that Blessed One Ṛṣabha, whose connection to material signs had thus been released, yet which still moved through this earth by means of a mere semblance of egoism due to the latent impressions of his yogic power (yogamāyā), arrived by chance in the regions of Koṅka, Veṅka, and Kuṭaka in Southern Karṇāṭaka; there, in the grove of Mount Kuṭaka, he sat chewing a mouthful of stone like one who was mad, with his hair disheveled.
He wandered about while still fully clothed.

Then, a fierce forest fire, born from the friction of bamboo stalks tossed by the force of the wind, began licking that forest and burned it along with him. Having heard his life story, the kings of Koṅka, Veṅka, and Kuṭaka indeed learned the name "Arhat."

In the Kali age, as unrighteousness increases, the dull-witted man, deluded by destiny, will abandon the path of his own dharma— which is free from fear on all sides— and, by his own intellect, promote a wicked, heretical, and inconsistent way.
Indeed, by this means, the lowest of men in the Kali age, bewildered by the illusory power of the Divine, will become devoid of their own prescribed duties, discipline, purity, and good conduct.

By their own individual whims, they will embrace acts of disrespect toward the gods and violations of sacred vows—such as neglecting ritual bathing, sipping water for purification, maintaining bodily cleanliness, and even the plucking out of hair.

With their intellects corrupted by the predominance of *kali* and unrighteousness, they will generally become revilers of the Vedas, the brāhmaṇas, the sacrificial rites, the Supreme Person, and the world itself.
And, satisfied with their own recent worldly ways—a blind tradition—they will themselves fall into the blinding darkness of ignorance.
This incarnation is for the purpose of instructing those who have fallen away from liberation due to the influence of passion (*rajas*).
Regarding this, they sing these corresponding verses:
"Oh, among the islands and regions of this earth which possesses seven oceans, this is the most meritorious!
The people of that place sing of the auspicious deeds of Murāri, which manifest his incarnations. Oh, how glorious is this lineage of Priyavrata, in which the ancient Person,
the Primeval Puruṣa who has taken incarnation, practiced that dharma which is not a cause for further action!
"Who else, indeed, could even with the wish of his mind follow to the ultimate limit of this unborn one,
the yogi who yearns for the *yoga-māyās* which have been cast aside by him through the realization of non-existence (unreality), despite their efforts?
Thus it was said concerning the Blessed One, the supreme teacher of all the Vedas, the world, the gods, the *brāhmaṇas*, and the cows.

The pure conduct of the one named Ṛṣabha has been described; it removes all the evil deeds of men and is the supreme abode of great auspiciousness. Whoever listens to this with well-accumulated faith, or causes others to hear it, being attentive toward that Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, in both of them devotion to Him alone continues to prevail.

In that very [devotion], the wise— who at every moment bathe their souls, which are incessantly tormented by the miseries of various worldly existences— do not even care for ultimate liberation (*apavarga*), the supreme goal of human life,
once it has been spontaneously attained; for, through their state of being the Lord’s own (*bhagavadīyatva*), all their purposes are completely fulfilled.

"O King, the Lord of the Yadus is your master, your guru, your deity, your beloved, and the protector of your lineage; how could he possibly be your servant? Yet, my dear friend, let it be so for those who worship the Blessed One, for Mukunda grants his grace to his devotees."
He may sometimes grant liberation, but never the yoga of devotion,
to one whose thirst for his own self— which is eternally experienced— is stilled,
yet whose intellect has long been asleep regarding the means to the highest good through the pursuit of what is not that.
Salutations to that Blessed One, the Bull among sages, who out of compassion revealed to the world the fearless realm of the Self. Śrī Śuka said:

But Bharata, the great devotee of the Lord, when he was appointed by the Blessed One to protect the surface of the earth, became intent on carrying out His instructions. He begot upon Pañcajanī, the daughter of Viśvarūpa, five sons who were entirely worthy of himself, just as the originator of the elements produces the subtle elements: Sumati, Rāṣṭrabhṛt, Sudarśana, Āvaraṇa, and Dhūmraketu.
This region named Ajanābha is called Bhārata, from which [the lineage] takes its designation.
That lord of the earth, who was very wise, protected his subjects—who were abiding in their respective duties—just as his own father and grandfather had done, out of great affection;

and he himself, following his own dharma, performed worship of the Blessed Lord in the form of sacrifice through various high and low rituals, including the Agnihotra, Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, Paśu, and Soma sacrifices, all offered with faith.
While various sacrifices were being performed at each pressing according to the ritual of the four officiating priests (*cāturhotra*),

with their constituent rites duly arranged through primary and secondary elements, that unprecedented fruit of action known as *dharma* was established within the Supreme Brahman, the Sacrificial Person (*yajña-puruṣa*), by virtue of His being the regulator of the meaning of all mantras containing the designations of the deities.

Meditating upon the Blessed Vāsudeva, the supreme deity who is the direct witness, that sacrificer— his impurities having been worn away by his own skillful practice— visualized those gods who partake in the sacrifice within the limbs of the Supreme Person as the oblations were being taken up by the Adhvaryu priests. Thus, for one whose inner being is purified through the purification of ritual action, [the Lord appears] within the body of the ether of the heart, in Brahman.
Toward the Blessed Vāsudeva— who is characterized by the form of the Great Person (mahā-puruṣa), distinguished by the Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, forest garland, lotus, discus, mace, and other emblems;
who shines in the form of a person within his own heart, which is inscribed with the image of that Person— there arose a supreme devotion, the intensity of which increased day by day.
Thus, when the opportunity for the cessation of his karma had reached its end after ten thousand times ten thousand years,

he divided the ancestral inheritance being enjoyed among his sons according to their respective shares; then, departing from his own abode— the dwelling-place of all prosperity— he set out for the hermitage of Pulaha.
In that very place, even today, the Blessed Lord Hari makes himself present through his affection for the local inhabitants by assuming their desired forms.
There, the excellent river named Cakranadī—whose waters flow from both sides through stone wheels marked with the Lord’s footprints—purifies everything on all sides.
It is there, indeed, in the grove of Pulaha’s hermitage, that he alone [performs his worship] with various flowers, sprouts, *tulasī*, and water.
Striving to worship the Blessed One with offerings of bulbs, roots, and fruits, living in solitude, having ceased his longing for sense objects,

and possessing a tranquility that was fully sustained, he attained supreme bliss. Thus, through his incessant service to the Person, his heart became softened by the weight of an ever-increasing surge of devotion toward the Blessed One.
With the force of intense joy causing his body to break out in a multitude of horripilations, and with his vision obstructed by tears of affection arising from longing,

his intellect— plunged into the deep lake of his heart which was overflowing with supreme bliss through the practice of devotional yoga (*bhakti-yoga*) consisting of constant meditation upon the lotus feet, as red as his own beloved,
no longer remembered even the worship of the Blessed One that was being performed.
Thus, having undertaken the vow of the Blessed One, he shone with a garment of deerskin and a mass of curly, tawny matted hair wet from his ritual ablutions at each of the three periods of the day;

as the solar disc was rising, he approached the golden Puruṣa, the Blessed One, while worshipping the sun, and spoke this: "O Jātavedas, beyond the dust of the world, the splendor of the divine Savitṛ has generated this [universe] through the mind."
Having entered again through the semen of a god, he beheld the Haṃsa; we pay homage to him who dwells in the vulture, in man, and in the Ṛg-verses.
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, having performed his ablutions and the obligatory daily duties in the great river, he sat for three muhūrtas on the water's edge, chanting the imperishable Brahman.
O King, at that time, a certain doe, driven by thirst, approached a body of water all alone. While she was drinking the water, the loud roar of a lion, terrifying to the world, arose nearby.
Hearing it, that female deer—naturally timid, with startled eyes, her heart intensely agitated by the obsession of fear for Hari, and her gaze darting about—[fled].
Out of fear of the thirst that had come upon her, she suddenly leaped up.

As she was springing upward, the fetus—which had already emerged from the womb—fell out and dropped into the stream due to the terror of her thighs. Afflicted by the exhaustion and fear of this premature birth, and being separated from her own herd, the black doe fell into a certain cave and then died.

Beholding that pitiable young deer being carried away by the current and abandoned, the royal sage Bharata, out of compassion like a kinsman, took it up and led it to his hermitage, saying, "It is motherless. Indeed,
for that young deer, which had developed a deep sense of self-identification with him, day after day...

Through constant meditation on nourishing, protecting, fondling, and pleasing him, their self-restraints along with the observances—such as service to the Supreme Person and so forth—were all indeed cast aside after being deprived for only a few days at a time.
"Alas! This fawn of Hari is so pitiable; by the speed of his wandering around the wheels of the Lord's chariot," [he cried].

Abandoned by his own group, friends, and kinsmen, and finding no other refuge, he has approached me alone as his mother, father, brothers, relatives, and companions; he knows no one else and places his full confidence in me. Therefore, knowing the fault of neglecting a seeker for refuge, I—being free from envy—must carry out the nourishing, protecting, pleasing, and cherishing of this one who is solely devoted to me.
"Truly, noble and virtuous persons whose nature is tranquility and who are friends to the distressed disregard even their own most important interests for the sake of such a purpose.
Thinking thus, he remained constantly attached in heart to Mṛgajihva through affection, accompanying him in sitting, lying down, walking, bathing, eating, and other activities.

When he went to the forest with the young deer to gather *kuśa* grass, flowers, sacrificial fuel, *palāśa* leaves, fruits, roots, and water, he was filled with apprehension regarding danger from wolves, jackals, and other predators.

And on the paths, with his mind and heart attached here and there by the weight of affection through a state of infatuation, he would carry him on his shoulder out of wretchedness; likewise, placing him on his lap or against his chest and fondling him, he attained supreme joy.
Even while the ritual was being performed, rising again and again during the intervals, whenever he would look upon him...
"Then indeed, that lord of the rains, with a mind established in its natural state, offered him blessings, saying: 'May it be well with you, my child, in every respect.
On another occasion, however, his mind was deeply agitated; like a wretched man who has lost his wealth, he spoke piteously, overwhelmed by excessive longing.

Alas! That poor young fawn, the son of a dead doe—will he not come here like a simple person, placing his trust in me, a base man of deceitful Kirāta intellect and unrighteous deeds, relying on his own confidence and disregarding my true nature?
Oh, will I see him, protected by the gods, grazing safely on the young grass in this hermitage grove?
Moreover, neither a wolf, nor a hyena, nor any other solitary predator will devour her;
for the Blessed One—the soul of the three Vedas and the source of welfare and prosperity for the entire world—is setting. Even now, the deposit of my fawn does not return.
Will the prince of deer-children, having come here, perhaps delight me with his various beautiful and charming fawns and dispel my dissatisfaction, even though he has performed no meritorious deeds?

While I was feigning deep meditation with eyes closed during a playful quarrel to drive away his own kinsmen, he approached me with great agitation out of love and rolled over me with the tip of his slightly blunt horn.
When the sacrificial grass upon which the oblation had been placed was defiled by me, he became terrified; immediately ceasing his dance, he remained with all his senses restrained like a young sage.

Or rather, what austerities must this ascetic woman have performed, such that this earth— by the rows of hoof-prints left by the very beautiful and most auspicious young son of the gentle black antelope— is indicating the path to wealth for me, a wretched man distressed by the loss of my riches, while simultaneously making herself a place of divine worship for the twice-born who desire heaven and liberation, adorned as she is with all manner of wonders?

Could it be that the Blessed Lord of the Stars, who is compassionate toward the wretched, out of pity has taken this young fawn— whose mother is dead and who has strayed from his own hermitage— out of fear of the king of beasts?

Or else, does he, whose lotus-like heart-lake is being scorched by the cresting flames of the forest-fire of fever born from separation from his son, nourish me with the nectar-filled rays of his own face, which are intensified by the cool, peaceful affection for the fawn that approached him?

Thus, with his heart agitated by unfulfilled desires, that ascetic practitioner of yoga was diverted from the commencement of yoga by the force of his own previously begun karma appearing as a young deer; for otherwise, how could he have developed such an attachment toward a fawn of another species— an attachment that is directly opposed to the highest good— for one whose noble heart had previously renounced what is so difficult to abandon?

While that royal sage Bharata was thus occupied with the constant attachment of nourishing, protecting, pleasing, and fondling the young fawn— neglecting his own self— the terrible onset of Time, as irresistible as a snake entering a rat's hole, arrived with its fierce impetuosity.
Even then, he beheld him grieving for the one standing by his side as if for his own son.

With his mind fixed solely on the deer, having abandoned this world along with the deer, he followed the dead body; yet, unlike others, he did not lose the memory of his previous birth and thus obtained the body of a deer.
Even there, indeed, having remembered the cause of his own state as a deer through the power of his desire to worship the Blessed One, he became deeply remorseful and said:

"Alas, what a tragedy! I have fallen from the path of the self-possessed, for my mind— which had been entirely absorbed and concentrated through the diligent practice of hearing, reflecting upon, glorifying, worshipping, and remembering the Blessed Vāsudeva, the Self of all selves, by one who has abandoned all attachments and takes refuge in the secluded, holy forest— has now, due to my ignorance, flowed away like water following a young deer."

Thus, with his inner despair concealed, he left his mother, the doe, and returned from Kālañjara to Śālagrāma— the hermitage of Pulastya and Pulaha, a sacred field of the Lord beloved by hosts of sages whose nature is tranquility— where he awaited the appointed time as his companion, deeply distressed by worldly association.
Subsisting on dry leaves, grass, and creepers, and counting only the end of his state as a deer, he cast off his deer body,
which had been moistened by the water of a sacred ford.
Śrī Śuka said:
Now, to a certain eminent brahmin of the Aṅgiras lineage—

who was endowed with tranquility, self-control, austerity, Vedic study, renunciation, contentment, forbearance, humility, learning, freedom from envy, and the bliss of self-knowledge— there were born nine uterine sons, equal to himself in learning, character, conduct, beauty, and noble qualities, as well as a pair of twins in his youngest wife; and he who was the male among them...
They say that Bharata, that most excellent royal sage and supreme devotee, having cast off his animal body, attained the state of a brāhmaṇa in his final body.

Even there, being greatly distressed by association with his own kinsmen, he [took refuge] in the pair of lotus feet of the Lord— the hearing, remembering, and description of whose qualities destroys the bondage of karma.

Fearing that his own life might be obstructed, he mentally devised a plan; and by the grace of the Blessed One, having recollected the succession of his previous births, he presented himself to the world in the form of one who was insane, dull-witted, blind, and deaf.
Indeed, the Brahmin, his mind bound by affection for his son, [watched] him until his return from the place of study.

Performing the sacraments according to the instructions, he further taught the initiated boy the ritual observances, such as purification and sipping water, even though they were not to his liking, thinking, "A son must be obedient to his father" (BhP 5.9.4). And he, for his part, acted as if contrary to that very instruction in the presence of his father regarding the Vedic meters (*chandas*).

Intending to teach him, he caused his son— who, though studying during the months of spring and summer, had not yet mastered the form of the three-footed Sāvitrī along with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *praṇava*, and the *śiras*— to grasp it.

Thus, his mind possessed by affection for his own son, [the father] [instructed him] in the duties of a student (*aupakurvāṇaka*), such as purity, study, vows, observances, service to the guru and the sacred fire, and so forth.

"Even those who are not diligent must be instructed"—this was his persistent attachment to what was untrue. Having thus instructed his son, he himself, failing to attain his heart's desire, was eventually taken away by time while remaining heedless at home despite his former vigilance.
Then the younger wife of the twice-born, having entrusted the twin children born from her womb to her co-wife, departed for the world of her husband by means of her own funeral rites.

When his father had passed away, his brothers— unaware of his spiritual power and with their minds fixed solely on the threefold Vedic knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) rather than the supreme knowledge (*para-vidyā*)— desisted from insisting on instructing their brother, thinking him to be dull-witted. And he was addressed by ordinary men, those cattle among bipeds, as "insane," "dull," "deaf," and "mute."

When he speaks words appropriate to that [state], and performs actions whether by the will of another, as a laborer, for wages, or by begging— whether what is obtained is small or great, choice food or coarse fare— he consumes it not for the sake of sensory gratification, but because he has attained the realization of his own Self, which is the bliss of pure, self-established experience, eternally free from all causal motives.
With no sense of bodily identification toward the duality of pleasure and pain,

he was like a bull with his body uncovered by cold, heat, wind, and rain; stout and possessed of well-knit limbs, his spiritual luster (brahma-varcasa) remained unmanifested due to sleeping on the bare ground, lack of massage, lack of bathing, and the dust [of his life], yet he was a twice-born man whose waist was covered by a tattered cloth and whose thighs were smeared with ash by his sacred thread.
Thus, despised by those who knew the truth because of his designation as a "brahma-bandhu" (a pseudo-Brahmin), he wandered about.

When, seeking food from others through the wages of labor, he was even appointed by his own brothers to work in the fields, he performed that task; however, he did not do it properly, but rather unevenly, deficiently, or excessively.
He consumed even fragments of Vedic hymns, oil-cakes, chaff, boiled grains, the dregs from a cooking pot, and so forth, as if they were nectar.

Then once, a certain lord of the low-born, desiring offspring, sacrificed a human victim to the goddess Bhadrakālī. While his followers were running after the tracks of that sacrificial animal, which had been released by fate, [they saw him].

At night, at the hour of midnight, when the darkness had enveloped everything, they saw the son of the best of the Aṅgirases protecting the fields from deer, boars, and other wild animals by means of the *vīrāsana* posture, according to an unexpected providence. Then, perceiving him to possess faultless marks and considering him to have accomplished their master’s task, they bound him with a rope and led him to the temple of Caṇḍikā with joyful, blossoming faces.

Then the sacrificers, having consecrated him according to their own ritual, clothed him in new garments, and adorned him with ornaments, unguents, garlands, and tilaka; and once he had eaten, they seated that human victim before Bhadrakālī with great singing, hymns, and the sound of mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas, accompanied by the sacrificial arrangement consisting of incense, lamps, garlands, parched grain, young shoots, sprouts, and fruit offerings.

Then the butcher of the Śūdra king, intending to sacrifice the goddess Bhadrakālī with the blood and wine of that human beast, took up a sword consecrated by mantras, which was exceedingly fierce and sharpened.
Thus, those Śūdras— whose natures were characterized by passion and ignorance (*rajas* and *tamas*), whose minds were intoxicated by the dust of wealth and pride,
who had treated the lineage of heroes descended from a portion of the Lord with contempt, who wandered at will along a pathless way, and whose pastimes were acts of violence— [acted].

Perceiving that most cruel deed— the slaughter in a slaughterhouse of one who was truly Brahman, the son of a Brahmarṣi, free from enmity, and a friend to all beings— Bhadrakālī herself, the goddess, suddenly leapt forth with a body burning with the utterly unbearable splendor of Brahman.

With her face rendered exceedingly terrifying by the violent knitting of her eyebrows and the fierce dilation of her copper-red eyes—features agitated by the forceful onset of intense indignation and wrath—she let out a loud, boisterous laugh in her desire to slay them. Then, springing up with great impetuosity, she drank, along with her retinue, the extremely hot wine of blood flowing from the necks of those wicked and evil ones whose heads had been severed by that very sword; and, overwhelmed by the intoxication of excessive drinking, she raised her voice even higher.

Together with his own attendants, he sang, danced, and sported, playing with his head as if it were a ball. Indeed, such a great transgression of malevolent magic bears fruit in its entirety upon oneself.
O Viṣṇudatta, this is no small wonder—that he remained unperturbed even at the severing of his own head.

Even when calamity has befallen them, those paramahaṃsa devotees of the Lord— who have loosened the firm knots of the heart regarding the self-identity of the body and so forth, who regard all beings as their own friends,
and who are free from enmity— are protected by various means by the Lord himself, who is vigilant and whose weapon is the enemy of the gods (Śiva).
Having approached the soles of his feet, they dwell there free from fear from any quarter.
Śrī Śuka said:
Now, O Lord of Sindhu-Sauvīra, as Rahūgaṇa was traveling along the bank of the Ikṣumatī,
at the time when he was searching for men to carry his palanquin, that best of the twice-born, who had been brought there by destiny, was found— this stout man.

Though he was not worthy of it, that noble-souled one was forcibly made to carry the palanquin along with those previously conscripted for labor, on the grounds that he was young, possessed a sturdy frame, and was capable of bearing the burden like an ox or a donkey; for when the movement of the men could not keep pace with his stride, which followed merely from the glance of that best of the twice-born, [the palanquin would stop].
Then, noticing that his palanquin was moving unevenly, Rahūgaṇa addressed the bearers: "O carriers, proceed properly!

Why is the vehicle being carried unevenly? (BhP 5.10.3). Then, hearing those words of the lord which were full of reproach, they became apprehensive—having reached their wits' end—and made this representation to him:

"O King, we are not negligent; we follow your commands and carry [the burden] quite well. Yet, even though he has just now been assigned, this one does not walk quickly, and indeed we are unable to carry it together with him.
"Surely, the fault of association belongs to all those who associate, even if it affects only one."

Having heard the piteous words of the woman and being certain that she was indeed an *arhatī*, King Rahūgaṇa—though he had served his elders and was naturally restrained—was forcibly moved by emotion;
with his mind clouded by passion, like a fire shrouded by smoke, he spoke with a slightly rising anger to her whose spiritual luster was not yet manifest:
"Alas, what a tragedy! O brother, you have clearly become utterly exhausted from traveling this long road all alone."

"O friend, you have carried [this body] for a very long time; you are neither excessively fat nor possessed of a compact frame, and you are not afflicted by old age. Indeed, there is no other such as you among these colliding beings. Though greatly deceived by ignorance, you have not superimposed the false notion of 'I' and 'mine' upon this insubstantial particular configuration—a mere aggregate of substance, quality, action, and latent impressions that constitutes your final body—and thus you have become Brahman."
He carried the palanquin silently as before.
Then, when his own palanquin again became unsteady, Rahūgaṇa, becoming enraged, said:
"What is this, you? Are you a living corpse, disregarding me and transgressing the command of your master while being so negligent?"
"And I shall provide you with such treatment as Daṇḍapāṇi does for the people, so that you will return to your own true nature," [said the Lord].

Thus, while he was speaking many such incoherent things— possessing the pride of a god among men, his entire devotion to the beloved abode of the Blessed One obscured by intoxication permeated by passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas), and considering himself a scholar— the Blessed Brāhmaṇa...

Having become one with Brahman, a friend to all beings, and his own self, he— free from pride and smiling as it were toward the sage whose mind was not overly proficient in the conduct of the Lord of Yoga— spoke this. The Brāhmaṇa said:
"What you have spoken is clear and not deceptive; O hero, he would indeed be my burden if he were the one to be supported by me.
If the goal were within reach of the traveler, there would be no saying among the wise that 'the path is long' when faced with a heavy load.
[For all beings,] there is bulkiness and leanness, diseases and mental anxieties, hunger and thirst, fear, strife, desire, and old age."
Sleep, pleasure, anger, egoism, intoxication, and sorrows—these do not exist for me who am born with a body.

O King, the state of being "living yet dead" is invariably observed in one who is subject to transformation, as it is seen to have a beginning and an end. That in which the relationship between master and servant is eternal and worthy of praise is indeed called the yoga of the performance of ordained duties.
We perceive only a slight opening for the notion of distinction, and nothing other than what arises from worldly convention.
Who there is a lord, and what is there to be ruled? Nevertheless, O King, what can we do for you?
O hero, for one like me who has attained his own true state, what is the use of medical treatment, as if for one who is insane, intoxicated, or an idiot?
"What possible purpose is served by your instruction? It is like grinding what is already ground for one who is arrogant and heedless.
Śrī Śuka said:

Having replied thus with this explanatory discourse, the best of sages, whose nature was tranquility and who had ceased identifying with the self as a cause, set out in a royal carriage while exhausting the karma already commenced through his experience.
And so he spoke (BhP 5.10.15): And that lord of Sindhu and Sauvīra, O son of Pāṇḍu, having been authorized by his office through perfect faith in the desire to know reality,
and having heard those words of the twice-born which loosen the knots of the heart and are approved by many Yoga treatises, quickly descended [from his chariot].
Approaching the soles of his feet with his head bowed and seeking forgiveness, he—his pride in kings and gods now vanished—said:
"Who are you that wander in disguise among the twice-born? You wear the sacred thread; which *avadhūta* are you? Whose disciple are you?
From where have you come? For what purpose are you here? Are you not our protector, for you do not appear to be one of us?"

I do not fear the thunderbolts of the king of the gods, nor the tridents of the three-eyed Śiva, nor the staff of Yama; I do not fear the weapons of Agni, Arka, Soma, Anila, or Vittapa. Yet, I am deeply afraid of the insult shown to the community of Brahmins.
Therefore, speak: you wander like one detached and dull-witted, yet you possess hidden power of wisdom and are boundless.
O virtuous one, these words of yours, woven with yoga, cannot be pierced by my mind even in thought.

And as for me, I have set out to ask the Lord of Yoga, who is the supreme teacher of the sages who know the reality of the Self—Him who has descended here as a mere fraction of His knowledge, Hari Himself. What is the purpose of this journey?
Surely Your Lordship wanders about with unmanifested marks for the sake of observing the world;

yet how could one of dull intellect and attachment to home perceive the path of the masters of yoga? I acknowledge that the exhaustion resulting from action was indeed seen in you, my master and protector, as you traveled.

Just as the worldly path of activity is considered to have its root in the absence of bringing and taking away what does not exist [in reality], so too, from the heat of the fire in the pot comes the heating of the milk; from that heating comes the cooking of the rice within it.
Similarly, through the contact of the body, senses, mind, and the internal organ (āśaya), the cycle of transmigration for the person (puruṣa) occurs in accordance with his own inclination.

The king is the teacher and protector of his subjects; he who is a servant indeed does not grind what is already ground. Striving to fulfill one's own duty as worship of Acyuta, one casts off the flood of sins.
Yet you, O King, have treated the most excellent of beings with contempt through the intoxication of pride in your status as a lord of men. Such is my situation.
O friend of the distressed, may You bestow upon me that vision of Your friendship, by which I may cross over this sin that obstructs the meditation on the Truth.
Even for You, the friend of all beings, there can be no transformation of state due to equanimity, as You are free from personal preferences;
yet, because of the great pride born of his own actions, even Śiva will soon perish along with those like me.
The brāhmaṇa said:
You speak the words of the learned while being yourself unlearned; yet you do not consider yourself the best among those who possess true knowledge.
For the wise do not regard this worldly discourse as consistent with the investigation of ultimate reality.

Likewise, O King, although the Vedic discourses have expanded greatly through the extensive ritual arrangements of householders skilled in the sacrificial system, the pure and perfect discourse on ultimate reality does not generally shine forth therein. Indeed,
even the most excellent words were not sufficient for him to directly grasp that reality.
In a dream, one might realize through reasoning that the happiness of a householder is not something to be abandoned;
yet as long as a person’s mind is constrained by passion (*rajas*), goodness (*sattva*), or ignorance (*tamas*),
it spreads forth unrestrainedly through thoughts and intentions, whether toward what is wholesome or otherwise.
That self, consisting of latent impressions and colored by sense objects, is a stream of the *guṇas* that has undergone transformation; comprising sixteen aspects,
it assumes various names and distinct forms according to its internal and external states, and through its cities (the body),
it expands and manifests the intense fruits of experience— pain, pleasure, and that which is beyond both— as they arise in due time.
Embracing his own embodied self through a mind fashioned by *māyā*, that deceiver of the wheel of worldly existence remains as he is;
this entire empirical process, whether gross or subtle, is always manifest and witnessed by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).
Therefore, they say that the mind is the indicator of the qualities and the absence of qualities, and of the higher and the lower.
The mind of a living being becomes attached to the modes of nature for its own ruin, whereas a state free from the modes leads to its well-being.

Just as a lamp, while consuming the ghee and the wick, emits smoky flames, yet at other times returns to its own true nature; so too the mind, bound by the qualities and their activities, resorts to various fluctuations, but elsewhere it rests in the Absolute Truth.

The eleven functions of the mind are indeed its modes of activity: the five perceptions, the intellect, and the ego; O hero, they say their spheres of action are the objects of the senses, the activities, and the body. These are: smelling, seeing, touching, tasting, and hearing; and excretion, sexual pleasure, aversion, speech, and manual skill.
The eleventh is appropriation, thinking "this is mine," and they say the twelfth is the bed;
these eleven modifications of the mind arise from substance, nature, intention, action, and time.
They occur by the thousands, hundreds, and crores through the conscious self (kṣetrajña), neither mutually nor independently.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) perceives these eternal manifestations of the mind belonging to the individual soul (jīva), which is fashioned by Māyā—manifesting in some places and disappearing in others—for he is pure while the agent is impure. The Knower of the Field is the Self, the Person, the Ancient One; he is directly self-luminous, unborn, and the Supreme Lord.

The Lord Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, concealing Himself within His own self by means of His own māyā, rules over all things— just as the wind, though pervading both the stationary and the moving through its own essential nature, exercises its power;
even so, the Supreme Lord Vāsudeva, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), has entered this [universe] as the Self.

O King, as long as this embodied being has not shaken off this illusion by the dawning of wisdom, and remains with attachments unsevered and the six enemies unsubdued, so long does he wander here, failing to realize the true nature of the Self through the Vedas.
As long as this mind— the indicator of the Self— is the field for sowing the seeds of worldly suffering for a person, [so long does he wander].

O heedful one, with the weapon of worshiping the feet of the Guru Hari, destroy this enemy who steals away the self— this formidable foe that manifests as possessiveness and is fueled by the continuous bonds of grief, delusion, disease, passion, greed, and enmity; destroy this falsehood through equanimity.
Rahūgaṇa said:
"Obeisances again and again to You whose form is the cause of all, who have rendered Your own true nature insignificant compared to Your manifested forms;
obeisances to You, the Avadhūta, who conceal Your eternal realization behind the external marks of a common brahmin."

O Brahmin, just as genuine medicine is for one afflicted by the disease of fever, or as cool water is for one scorched by the summer heat, so your words are nectar and medicine for me, whose vision has been bitten by the serpent of pride regarding this wretched body.
Therefore, I shall ask you later about my doubt; for now, please speak what is easily understood.
Please explain to me, whose mind is filled with curiosity, that which was spoken by You regarding the spiritual yoga (*adhyātma-yoga*), for You,
O Lord of Yoga, have said that what is perceived is the fruit of action and the root of worldly conduct; indeed,
my mind does not readily turn toward the investigation of reality in this regard.
The brāhmaṇa said:
O King, for what reason does this person, who moves upon the earth, exist as a ruler?
Even for him, there are the ankles, shanks, knees, thighs, waist, neck, and shoulders situated above his feet.
Upon your shoulder rests the palanquin made of wood, in which sits the one who bears the title "King of Sauvīra.

You, blinded by the intoxication of pride, have developed a deep-seated egoism therein, thinking, "I am the king among the Sindhus. By oppressing these wretched and miserable people with forced labor, you are utterly devoid of compassion.
Boasting, "I am the protector of the people," you do not shine in the assemblies of the elders, being so impudent.
Since we know that on this earth the origin and the ultimate end of all moving and non-moving beings are eternal,
let that which is other than the name— the root of worldly transaction— be investigated through the evidence of actual action.

Thus has been explained the etymological function of the word *kṣiti*. Those atoms which are non-existent yet imagined by the mind through ignorance— the specific distinctions created by their aggregate—
consist of the minute and the gross, the subtle and the vast, the unreal and the real, the living and the insentient, and all else.
Know that the second [state] is created by the names of material substance, inherent nature, intention, time, and action, and is subject to change.
But the first is pure knowledge, the singular supreme reality, immediate, internal, the externalless Brahman, the truth—
what the wise call Vāsudeva, known by the name of the Blessed Lord, who is inward-facing and perfectly tranquil.

O Rahūgaṇa, this state is not attained by austerity, nor by sacrifice, nor by the distribution of gifts from one's home, nor by Vedic hymns, nor even by water, fire, or the sun— without the sprinkling of the dust from the feet of the Great One,
wherein the chanting of the qualities of the Lord of Excellent Renown is commenced and worldly talk is suppressed.
When practiced daily by one desiring liberation, it bestows a virtuous mind upon Vāsudeva. Formerly, I was a king named Bharata, whose attachment to what is seen and heard had been severed;
while striving for the propitiation of the Lord, I became a deer through association with deer, thereby losing my purpose.
O hero, that remembrance of Kṛṣṇa’s worship, born from my devotion, does not leave me even while I am in the body of a deer.

Therefore, though unattached, I wander about with caution, never revealing myself due to my association with people. Thus, a person whose delusion has been severed right here by the sword of knowledge born from the excellent company of the unattached—
