Having regained his memory through hearing and narrating the activities of Hari, he reaches the further shore of the path.
The brāhmaṇa said:
On this path difficult to traverse, one is placed by Ajā (Māyā), with one's perception of action divided according to the modes of passion, ignorance, and goodness.
This caravan, intent on material gain, wanders through the forest of worldly existence and finds no peace.
O King, in this forest these six robbers forcibly plunder the caravan that has a poor leader;
there, jackals seize the traveler who is heedless, just as wolves enter a pen and carry off the sheep.
Harassed by fierce-biting mosquitoes in a thicket of abundant creepers, grasses, and shrubs,
he sometimes perceives a city of Gandharvas, and at other times, a blazing firebrand moving swiftly;
with the deluded notion that his dwelling, water, wealth, and self are there, he runs hither and thither in the forest.
In some places, his eyes clouded by dust, he cannot discern the directions which are smoky with the dust raised by whirlwinds;
with his inner self distressed by the cries of owls and the ear-piercing sounds of crickets that are barely visible, he,
tormented by hunger, takes refuge under unwholesome trees and runs toward mirages of water.
In some places he approaches waterless rivers and strives in vain to cross them;
in others, having encountered a forest fire, he is tormented by the flames; and in yet other places, his life-breath is snatched away by *yakṣas*.
In some instances his wealth is seized by robbers, and with a despondent mind, grieving and bewildered, he falls into utter dejection.

At times, having entered a city of the Gandharvas, he rejoices for a moment as if liberated; at other times, his feet pierced by thorns and pebbles while seeking to climb a mountain, he remains dejected. Afflicted at every step by the internal fire of worldly attachment, the householder indeed becomes angry with people.

In one place, a person swallowed by a python in the forest knows nothing as he lies cast away; and in another, bitten by venomous serpents, he sleeps blind in a dark well. At some time, searching for the flavors of the base, he is tormented and deprived of his senses by the flies that swarm around him.
There, obtaining [food] with extreme difficulty, others forcibly plunder it from him;
at times he remains unable to counteract cold, heat, wind, or rain;
and sometimes, by bartering with one another, he incurs hatred due to dishonesty regarding his wealth.

In some places or others, his wealth being exhausted, he was deprived of beds, seats, dwellings, and pastimes; begging from others without obtaining his desires, his gaze fixed upon the property of others, he suffered humiliation. Furthermore, through the mutual entanglement of their possessions, their enmity grew, and they married one another.
On that path, wandering amidst calamities, afflictions, and the loss of great wealth, one perishes;

for that caravan, abandoning those who have perished here and there and taking hold of whoever is born [along the way], continues its journey even today. O heroes, no one reaches the end of this path of yoga.
All those on earth who possess intelligence and have conquered the lordly elephants of the quarters harbor the notion "this is mine" and remain bound by enmity;
they may lie dead in battle, yet they do not attain that state which one reaches when, having laid down the rod of punishment and being free from enmity, one approaches [the Lord].
One who takes refuge in the creeper-like arms [of the Lord] becomes attached to something else, desiring the twice-born birds whose station is unmanifest and dependent upon that very refuge.
Sometimes, out of fear of the discus of Hari, he forms friendships with cranes, herons, and vultures;
deceived by them, he enters the flock of swans, yet finding no pleasure in their character, he approaches the monkeys.
Finding great satisfaction among his own kind, his senses are fully contented, and through gazing at one another, he forgets the appointed time limit.

Delighting among the trees, affectionate toward his children and wife, yet distressed by sexual desire and helpless in his own bondage, he once fell by chance into a mountain cave; there, terrified of the elephant, he remained clinging to a creeper. O subduer of enemies, having somehow escaped that calamity, he entered a caravan once again.
On this path, placed there by the Unconquered One (Māyā), no person wandering even today knows [the truth].
O Rahūgaṇa, you too, having laid down the rod [of punishment], having cultivated friendliness toward all beings,
and having fixed your self in the unreal, shall cross to the further shore by taking up the sharp sword of knowledge through service to Hari.
The King said:

"Aha! Human birth is the most auspicious of all births; what is the use of other births if one does not have the abundant company of you great souls, who have dedicated your very selves to the glory of Dhṛṣīkeśa?"

It is no wonder that those whose sins have been destroyed by the dust of Your lotus feet possess pure devotion to Adhokṣaja; for by even a moment’s association with You, my lack of discrimination—which is rooted in evil reasoning—has been cast away. Salutations to the great ones, salutations to the children, salutations to the youths, and salutations to the elders.
"May there be welfare for the kings from those brāhmaṇas who wander about disguised as avadhūtas.
Śrī Śuka said:
"O son of Uttarā, having thus spoken to the lord of Sindhu, that son of a brahmarṣi [revealed] the true nature of the self..."
As he was considering the other’s power, the Lord, out of supreme compassion, instructed him; his feet were then reverently saluted by Rahūgaṇa with tears of pity.
With the waves of his senses and the depths of his mind stilled like a full ocean, He wandered upon this earth.

(BhP 5.13.25) The lord of Sauvīra also, having understood the true nature of the Supreme Self from the assembly of saintly men, cast off the notion of identifying the self with the body—a notion superimposed upon the self by ignorance. O King, such indeed is the power of one who takes refuge in those who have taken refuge in the Blessed Lord.
The King said:

O great devotee, that path of worldly existence which you have described here with indirect words as being known by the learned is indeed one whose objects are fashioned by noble-minded sages; it is not easily understood by those who are unrefined.
"Now, let this very same [reality], which is difficult to comprehend, be explained by means of a synthesis of the various methods," he said.

"This very one [is perceived] through the series of diverse bodies constructed by the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome actions, which are differentiated by the specific qualities of *sattva* and the other *guṇas* of those who identify the body as the self."

By means of the group of six sense organs, which serves as the gateway to the experience of beginningless saṃsāra consisting of separation, union, and so forth, this world of living beings has fallen upon that path as difficult to traverse as a rugged mountain track; under the influence of the Māyā of the Lord, the Blessed Viṣṇu,
it is like a caravan of merchants intent on wealth, experiencing the fruits of actions performed by their own bodies, [and moving] like a cremation ground.

Having entered this most inauspicious forest of saṃsāra, I have not yet attained the path of the honey-bees at the lotus feet of Hari and the Guru— the path that pacifies all those torments— despite my many fruitless efforts and struggles.
For in this forest, these six senses, though called by such names, are indeed robbers through their actions.

Just as whatever wealth a man possesses that is conducive to dharma and acquired through great hardship— that dharma which is characterized by the direct worship of the Supreme Person— is called *sāmparāya* (pertaining to the hereafter); yet, by means of seeing, touching, hearing, tasting, smelling, imagining, resolving, and the enjoyment of home and sensual pleasures, those who lack a true protector and have no self-control plunder that wealth dedicated to dharma, just as they would plunder a caravan.

Moreover, in this world, the members of a family—wife, children, and so forth—are in name and deed nothing but wolves and jackals; they snatch away, even while the miserly householder looks on, that which he seeks to protect like a lamb, though he is unwilling to let it go.
For just as a field whose seeds have not been burnt returns again, even though it is ploughed every year.

Just as a field becomes overgrown with shrubs, grasses, and creepers at the time of sowing, so too is the householder’s life a field of action in which deeds never cease; for this dwelling is a casket of desires.
Having entered there, one is beset by base men who are like gadflies and mosquitoes, and by locusts, birds, thieves, mice, and the like.
With his external life-breaths obstructed and wandering somewhere along this path, he— whose mind is tainted by ignorance, desire, and karma—
perceives through a false vision the human world, which is actually unattainable, as if it were an attainable city of Gandharvas (a mirage).
And there, in some places, being greedy for the vices of drinking, eating, sexual intercourse, and so forth, he rushes toward sense-objects that resemble water in the heat of the sun.

Sometimes, his mind fixed on the color and qualities of a particular piece of excrement as the abode of all defects, he desires to seize that gold, like one distressed by the desire for fire who mistakes a firebrand for a demon.
Then, at other times, with an intense attachment to various means of livelihood such as shelter, water, and wealth, he runs hither and thither in this forest of worldly existence.

And sometimes, mounted upon a woman who is like a whirlwind, he— his boundaries of conduct rendered unrighteous by her passion (rajas) which makes him as if turned to night, his eyes reddened by passion, and his mind exceedingly clouded by passion— does not recognize the deities of the directions. At other times, having once understood the falsity of sense objects, yet with his memory corrupted by the constant contemplation of others, he runs after those very same objects as if they were mere mirages.
Sometimes, with his ears and heart deeply pained by the direct or indirect insults of hostile royal families— sounds as harsh, impetuous, and arrogant as the cries of owls and crickets— he,

when his previous merits have been exhausted, pursues those who are dead while living and whose wealth is devoid of both this-worldly and other-worldly purpose, like one drinking poison from trees and creepers such as the *kāraskara* and *kākatuṇḍa*, which are themselves as useless as they are deadly.
While he himself is dying, he seeks them out as if they were still alive.
Once, his intellect corrupted by association with the sixty-four arts, he pursues heretical paths that bring misery from both sides, like one stumbling in a stream whose current has been diverted;

when, blinded by the injury of others, he does not benefit himself, he indeed devours his own father, son, and sacrificial priests, or rather, his father and sons. Having at times reached a home that, like a forest fire, is devoid of beloved objects and results in unhappiness, he is intensely consumed by the fire of grief and falls into profound despondency.
Sometimes, when his beloved wealth and life-breath have been snatched away by the demons of time, disease, and the royal court, he remains like a corpse, devoid of the signs of life.
At other times, he experiences the semblance of satisfaction found in a dream, regarding his deceased fathers and grandfathers—who had come to him through his desires—as if they were real.

Sometimes, seeking to climb the mountain of the heavy burden of duties prescribed for the householder's stage of life, his mind exhausted by the world's miseries, he sinks down as if entering a field filled with thorns and pebbles.
At times, his vital essence seized by the unbearable internal fire of the body, he becomes angry even with his own family.
Again, seized by the python of sleep and plunged into blinding darkness, he lies like one in a desolate forest; cast away like a corpse, he knows nothing else at all.

Sometimes, his fangs of pride broken by the venomous snakes of wicked people, finding no moment of sleep and his consciousness wasting away with a pained heart, he is like a blind man in a blind well.
Whenever one, seeking the mere fragments of the honey of desire, seizes the wives or the wealth of others, he is slain by the king or his masters and falls into a shoreless hell.
Moreover, for both reasons, they declare that action in this world is the sowing of the self’s future existence.
Even if Devadatta is released from that bondage, Viṣṇumitra cuts him down from there as well; thus, there is no finality.

In some instances, being incapable of warding off the ten types of suffering—arising from the divine, the elemental, and the personal, such as cold, wind, and so forth—he remains despondent with endless anxiety.

In other instances, while engaging in mutual dealings, he may seize even a mere kārṣāpaṇa or a kākīṇikā of wealth from others, or he incurs some form of enmity through his stinginess regarding possessions.

On that path, there are these afflictions: pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, fear, pride, negligence, madness, grief, delusion, greed, envy, jealousy, arrogance, hunger, thirst, mental distress, disease, birth, old age, death, and so forth.

Somewhere, embraced by the vine-like arms of a woman through the divine illusion (*deva-māyā*), his discrimination and discernment have fallen away; his heart is agitated by the undertaking of building pleasure-houses for her, and his mind is stolen by the speech, glances, and gestures of the sons, daughters, and wives to whom he is attached.
One whose self is unconquered casts himself into the shoreless, blinding darkness;
for at some time, by the force of the revolving age— characterized by durations from a minute atom up to two *parārdhas*—
which sweeps away all beings from Brahmā down to blades of grass and stumps with unblinking speed, even as they look on.
With a terrified heart, disregarding that very Lord— the Supreme Person of Sacrifice (Yajña-puruṣa) who wields the wheel of time as His own weapon—
he instead addresses by conventional designations those heretical deities who are like hawks, vultures, cranes, and crows, and who are shunned by the noble tradition.
When he was thus greatly deceived by those self-deceived heretics, he entered into the community of the Brahmins.

They took pleasure only in the propitiation of the Lord, the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), through the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and the observance of moral conduct (*śīla*). They frequented the company of *śūdras*, for whom—due to their impurity according to the conduct prescribed by the Vedas—the act of sexual union was for the sake of maintaining a family, just as it is among the species of monkeys.

Even there, moving about unrestrainedly at will, they were of extremely wretched intellect; having forgotten the limits of time through vulgar acts such as gazing at one another's faces, they remained there.
Sometimes, like a monkey, he delights in his home for the sake of worldly objects, being affectionate toward his children and wife and intent on sexual union;
thus, like one traveling on a road, he wanders through a darkness resembling mountain caves out of fear of the elephant of death.

At times, he remains despondent over sense-objects that lead to endless suffering, being incapable of warding off the various sufferings—divine, elemental, and personal—such as cold, wind, and the like.
In some cases, he engages in mutual disputes and acquires whatever wealth he can through financial dishonesty;

in other cases, his wealth being exhausted, deprived of the enjoyment of beds, seats, food, and so forth, and with his mind fixed on seizing what has come to him despite his unfulfilled desires, he receives insults and the like from people here and there.

Thus, although the continuity of enmity has increased through the entanglement with wealth, one still marries and then divorces due to past impressions (*vāsanā*). On this path of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-adhvani*), afflicted by various sufferings and calamities, where one meets with success or meets with ruin, one indeed abandons one person there and takes up another as they are born; thus, grieving, deluded, fearing, and disputing, one wanders on.

Crying out, rejoicing, singing, and being bound, this caravan of the human world— from which point it was first set in motion— does not turn back even today, though they point to the further shore of that path. This instruction in yoga, which even those sages who have laid down the rod of violence, whose nature is tranquility, and whose selves are stilled do not fully attain, is not found here.

Furthermore, even those royal sages who were performers of sacrifices and conquerors of the elephants of the quarters eventually lay down upon this very earth in battle; having abandoned their bodies after forming a persistent enmity over the thought "this [earth] is mine," they were themselves withdrawn [by death].
Having clung to the creeper of karma, they were somehow liberated from calamities and hell, yet remaining once again on this path of saṃsāra, they enter the caravan of the human world.
Even though he had thus ascended higher,
they sang this of him:
"Of that great-souled royal sage Ārṣabha, even in his mind..."

A king does not deserve to follow after one who has renounced his wife, children, friends, and kingdom— things difficult to abandon yet dear to the heart— just as a fly cannot follow a soaring eagle; for he, longing for the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), cast them off like filth even while still young.

The King did not desire those things difficult to abandon— son, kin, wealth, and wife— nor did he seek the coveted prosperity that even the best of gods look upon with compassion; rather, he chose what was fitting for the great, O enemy of Madhu.
For those whose minds are devoted to service, even non-existence (liberation) is insignificant compared to him who is the goal of sacrifice, the Lord of Dharma, the master of ritual injunctions,
the head of Yoga and Sāṅkhya, and the Lord of Prakṛti.
He who, even while in the state of a deer, uttered the sublime words, "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, to Hari";
and he who [describes] this life-story of the royal sage Bharata, whose pure qualities and deeds were honored by the assembly of devotees.
One who hears, recounts, or rejoices in [this account], which brings well-being, longevity, wealth, fame, heaven, and liberation,
attains all blessings for himself and none at all from another.
Thus spoke Śrī Śuka.

Bharata’s son was named Sumati; indeed, some heretics will follow his path, while ignoble men, through their most wicked ingenuity in the Kali age, will invent a deity not mentioned in the Vedic recensions. From him, in the womb of Vṛddhasenā, a son named Devatājin was born.
Then his son was Asurya; from him was born Devadyumna, who begot a son, Parameṣṭhin, upon Dhenumatī. To Parameṣṭhin, Suvarcalā gave birth to Pratīha.

Having taught the science of the Self (Ātmavidyā), he himself became completely purified and meditated upon the Supreme Person (Mahāpuruṣa). From Pratīha and Suvarcalā were born three sons, Pratihartṛ and the others, who were experts in sacrificial rites. From Pratihartṛ and Stutī were born Aja and Bhūman.

From Bhūman was born Udgītha by Ṛṣikulyā; from him, Prastāva was born by Devakulyā; from Prastāva, Vibhu was born by Niyutsā; from Vibhu, Pṛthuṣeṇa was born by Ratī; from him, Nakta was born by Ākūti;
and from Nakta was born Druti’s son Gaya, a preeminent royal sage of noble fame, who was a direct manifestation of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.

Having attained the state of a Great Person (mahā-puruṣatā) through characteristics such as possessing a portion of the Self while having assumed the nature of a living being out of a desire to protect the world, he—by means of his own duty characterized by protecting, nourishing, pleasing, cherishing, and instructing the subjects, as well as by worship and other rites;

and by the yoga of devotion to the Lord, which was brought about through service to the feet of the Knower of Brahman and which consists of the dedication of the supreme goal with one's whole being to the Blessed One, the Great Person, the Supreme and the Lower Brahman—the [Lord]... [is pleased].

With a mind purified by constant cultivation and having transcended the notion of selfhood, he protected the earth while remaining entirely free from pride, even though he personally experienced the realization of Brahman as the Self within his own soul.
O descendant of Pāṇḍu, those who know the past sing this verse concerning him:
Who among kings can equal Gaya in his ritual sacrifices, his pride in performing them, his vast knowledge, his protection of dharma,
his attainment of prosperity, his presiding over assemblies, his devotion to the virtuous, and his service to the saintly— save for one who possesses even a fraction of the Lord’s power?
Him the chaste daughters of Dakṣa, whose blessings are ever true, joyfully consecrated with the waters of their rivers.

For him, the earth— whose udders were milked by the virtues [of his subjects] as her calf— yielded the blessings of his people, even though he himself was free from desire; and for him who had no personal longings, the Vedas yielded all desired objects, while the kings brought him tribute,
having approached him in battle with their weapons averted through righteousness, and having surrendered a sixth part of their sacrificial fees to the Brahmins.

At whose sacrifice the Lord, the soul of the ritual, rejoices at the abundant drinking of soma in the presence of Maghavat; and who, through the yoga of devotion purified by faith and offered as a sacrifice, brought forth the fruit of worship;
and by whose gratification, from the sacrificial grass down to the gods, animals, humans, plants, and grasses, all the way up to Viriñca, are satisfied.
He, the soul of all living beings, was immediately pleased; being pleased himself, he bestowed his own affection upon Gaya.
From Gaya and Gayantī were born three sons: Citraratha, Sugati, and Avarodhana.
From Citraratha and Ūrṇā was born Samrāṭ; from him and Utkalā was born Marīci; and from Marīci and Bindumatī...

A drop (bindu) was produced; from that, there arose one named Madhu among the *saraghā* bees. From Madhu, Vīravrata was born in Sumanas. From him, Manthu and Pramanthu were born of Bhojā. From Manthu, Bhauvana was born of Satyā. From Tvaṣṭṛ, he was born of Dūṣaṇā. From Tvaṣṭṛ, Viraja was born of Virocanā. From Viraja, there was a hundred sons, of whom Śatajit was the foremost, as well as a daughter.
And it is said that he was born from Viṣūcī;
regarding this, there is the following verse:
"The son born last from Viraja [became] this lineage of Priyavrata."
Viṣṇu has rendered the host of gods utterly insignificant by his fame.
The King said:
You have described the specific extent of the terrestrial sphere, as far as the sun shines and where the moon is seen together with the hosts of luminaries.

There too, by the seven moats formed by the tracks of Priyavrata’s chariot wheels, seven oceans were fashioned; since you, O Blessed One, have indeed indicated this differentiation of its seven islands,
I wish to understand all of this in its entirety, both according to its measurement and its characteristics.

"The mind, having been absorbed into the gross form of the Blessed One which consists of the modes of nature, is indeed capable of being absorbed even into the subtlest, quality-less light of the Self, the Supreme Brahman known as the Blessed Vāsudeva; therefore, O Guru,
you ought to describe that for me."
The sage said:

"O Great King, it is not possible for a person, even with a lifespan equal to that of the gods, to fully comprehend the limit of the Lord’s manifestations through the qualities of *māyā* by means of either mind or speech; therefore, [I shall describe] the specific features of the terrestrial globe according to their primary importance."
We shall explain [this] by way of the characteristics of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*) and pride (*māna*):
This island, which is like the interior calyx of a blue lotus bud, is a million *yojanas* in extent and is perfectly circular like a lotus leaf;
upon it there are nine regions (*varṣa*), each nine thousand *yojanas* in length, well-distinguished by eight boundary mountains.

Among these, the central region named Ilāvṛta is situated at the navel [of the earth], where Meru— the king of the principal mountain ranges, made entirely of gold, equal in height and breadth to the extent of the continent, and serving as the pericarp of the earth-lotus—
is located upon its summit; it is thirty-two thousand *yojanas* wide at the top and sixteen thousand at its base, penetrating the interior of the earth by that same measure.

To the north of Ilāvṛta are the three boundary mountains—Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān—which demarcate the regions (varṣas) of Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya, and Kuru. These mountains extend eastward, reaching as far as the salt ocean on both sides, and are two thousand yojanas wide each. Each successive mountain to the north is ten percent longer in length than the one preceding it.

Thus, to the south of Ilāvṛta, there are Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himālaya, extending eastward with heights of ten thousand yojanas, just as Nīla and the others do for the regions of Hari-varṣa, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata.
Similarly, to the west and east of Ilāvṛta, Mālyavat and Gandhamādana extend from Nīla to Niṣadha, spreading two thousand yojanas and establishing the boundaries of Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva.

Mandara, Merumandara, Supārśva, and Kumuda—these supporting mountains, ten thousand yojanas in both breadth and height, are fashioned on the four sides of Mount Meru. Upon these four mountains stand four preeminent trees—the mango, the jambū, the kadamba, and the nyagrodha—which, like the banners of the mountains, rise to a height of over a thousand yojanas and have branches spreading out to the same extent.

O bull of the Bharatas, there are four lakes with waters as sweet as milk, honey, sugarcane juice, and nectar; by touching them, the hosts of secondary deities (upadeva-gaṇas) maintain their natural powers of yoga and sovereignty. There are also four divine gardens—Nandana, Caitraratha, Vaibhrājaka, and Sarvatobhadra—in which the lords of the immortals sport together with the choicest of the celestial damsels, their greatness celebrated by the songs of the hosts of secondary deities.
On the slopes of Mount Mandara, fruits as large as mountain peaks fall from the tops of the celestial *devacūta* trees, which rise eleven hundred *yojanas* high; these fruits are like nectar.
As they shatter, their exceedingly sweet, fragrant, and abundant reddish juice flows down from the summit of Mount Mandara as a river named Āruṇodā, which flows eastward through Ilāvṛta.
By the mere enjoyment of which the wind, fragrant from contact with the limbs of the holy wives of her attendants, perfumes ten *yojanas* on all sides;
and likewise, by the juice of the *jambū* fruits— which fall from great heights and shatter, becoming almost boneless and resembling the bodies of elephants—
the river named Jambū flows from the peaks of Meru and Mandara for ten thousand *yojanas*, descending to the surface of the earth and flowing southward past itself.
As long as [the water] flows over Ilāvṛta,
the clay on both its banks, being permeated by that essence and ripened by the conjunction of wind and sun, becomes the gold named Jāmbūnada, which is the ornament of the world of the gods.
Indeed, that which the gods and others wear together with their young wives in the form of ornaments such as crowns, bracelets, and waist-bands— namely,

that great *kadamba* tree rooted on Supārśva— is such that from its hollows there issue five streams of honey, five in length and circumference, which fall from the peak of Supārśva and bring joy to Ilāvṛta, which lies to the west of them.
For the breath exhaled from the mouths of those who partake of its fruits perfumes everything for a hundred *yojanas* on all sides;
likewise, from the branches of that banyan tree named Śatavalśa which grows upon the Kumuda mountain,
there flow downward all things that yield every desire— milk, curds, honey, clarified butter, molasses, food, clothing, beds, seats, ornaments, and so forth.
The rivers falling from the summit of Kumuda provide for that region of Ilāvṛta to the north;
for those people who enjoy them, there never arise at any time afflictions such as wrinkles, gray hair, fatigue, perspiration, foul odors, old age, disease, death, cold, heat, discoloration,
or calamities— only lifelong, unsurpassed happiness.

The twenty mountains— Kuraṅga, Kurara, Kusumbha, Vaikaṅka, Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, Rucaka, Niṣadha, Śinīvāsa, Kapila, Śaṅkha, Vaidūrya, Jārudhi, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Nāga, Kālañjara, and Nārada— are situated all around the base of Meru like filaments surrounding its pericarp.
To the east of Meru, the Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa mountains extend eighteen thousand yojanas toward the north.
The two [peaks] Pṛthu and Tuṅga are two thousand [yojanas] in extent; likewise, to the west are Pavana and Pāriyātra, and to the south are Kailāsa and Karavīra, extending eastward;
similarly, to the north are Triśṛṅga and Makara. Encircled by these eight, the Golden Mountain shines on all sides like a fire.
On the summit of Mount Meru, they say there is a city fashioned from gold, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent and perfectly square, situated in the center of the Lord’s own abode.

Around it, in each direction, eight cities have been constructed for the eight guardians of the worlds, each measuring one-quarter of the central city and corresponding to the form of its respective guardian.
Śrī Śuka said:

There, after a vast period of time characterized by a thousand yugas, that stream which had entered through the opening of the upper shell of the cosmic egg—pierced by the toenail of the left big toe of the Lord Viṣṇu, who is the manifest emblem of sacrifice—as it flowed out, was colored by the reddish filaments from the washing of His lotus feet; it was capable of removing the stains of sin from the entire world through its mere contact, and was thus called by the name "the direct foot-stream of the Blessed One" (Bhagavat-padī). This was proclaimed by one whose speech was beyond perception.
That which they call the "footstep of Viṣṇu" is that which descended upon the summit of heaven.

There, indeed, the son of Uttānapāda, who was firm in his vows as a hero and a supreme devotee of the Lord, [dwelt], his inner heart constantly moistened by the ever-increasing yoga of devotion to the Lord— [the water] from the lotus feet of the deity of our own lineage, which he drank at every session.

Even now, with the utmost reverence, he bears upon his head that [lotus] from which pure tears trickle from the buds of his pair of eyes— eyes closed helplessly by intense longing— and which manifests a multitude of horripilations;
for it was indeed the ultimate fruit of his asceticism, as the seven sages well knew its power.

Such is the perfection attained by those who, through the acquisition of uninterrupted *bhakti-yoga* toward the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the Self of all, have disregarded all other goals and states of being;
like those seeking liberation who have reached liberation itself, they even today carry it with great honor in masses of matted locks.
Then, descending on a celestial vehicle crowded with many thousands of millions of chariots, she obscures the orb of the moon and alights at the abode of Brahmā.

There, dividing into four streams under four names, she flows toward the four directions and enters the lord of rivers (the ocean). These are the Sītā, Alakanandā, Cakṣu, and Bhadrā. The Sītā, flowing downward from the abode of Brahmā over the peaks of mountains such as Kesara, falls upon the summits of Gandhamādana and, passing through the middle of the region of Bhadrāśva, enters the salt ocean in the eastern direction.

Thus, flowing from the Mālyavat peak with unabated velocity, she enters the lord of rivers in the western direction toward Ketumāla. And the Bhadrā, having fallen from the summit of Meru in the north, passing from mountain peak to mountain peak,
flows down from the peak of Śṛṅgavān and enters the ocean in the northern direction toward the Northern Kurus.

In the same way, the Alakanandā flows from the abode of Brahmā toward the south; passing over many mountain peaks from Hemakūṭa, she washes away the golden summits with an exceedingly impetuous force and enters the ocean in the southern direction, showering upon the land of Bhārata.
In her, for every step taken by a man who comes for the purpose of bathing, there is the merit of the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, and other sacrifices.
"The fruit is not difficult to attain" (BhP 5.17.10).
Furthermore, there are many other rivers and streams in every region; indeed, there are hundreds of daughters of the mountains such as Meru.

Among them, Bhārata alone is the field of action (*karma-kṣetra*); the other eight regions are designated as terrestrial heavens (*bhaumāni svarga-padāni*), places for the enjoyment of the remaining merit of those who have resided in heaven.

Among these beings— who have a lifespan of ten thousand years, who are like gods, whose vital strength is that of ten thousand elephants, and whose wives conceive only once after a year due to sexual union characterized by great passion, joy, and delight, with bodies as firm as adamant— the time there proceeds like the Tretā Yuga.
There, the lords of the gods, having been honored with magnificent offerings by their respective leaders of the hosts, dwell in forest groves, hermitages,

temples, mountain valleys, and lakes of pure water— where the trees and creepers bend under the beauty of clusters of flowers, fruits, and sprouts from all seasons— and which are filled with royal swans, water-fowls, ducks, cranes, ruddy geese, and other birds, delighted by the fragrance of various blooming fresh lotuses.

In those regions, which resound with the humming of swarms of bees, the minds and eyes of the most charming celestial beauties are captivated by the playful glances, laughter, and amorous dalliances of the gods during their various diversions such as water-sports; there they roam at will.

Furthermore, throughout all nine regions, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, remains present even today through His own manifestation of the principles of the Self (ātma-tattva-vyūha) for the sake of bestowing grace upon the people.

In Ilāvṛta, however, the Lord Bhava alone is the sole male; indeed, no other enters there, for he knows the cause of Bhavānī’s curse—that whoever enters shall subsequently undergo a female state, which I shall describe later. Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of crores of female attendants belonging to the Lord of Bhavānī, [he remains] from the Blessed One...

Having brought into close proximity his own fourth, tamasic form as Prakṛti, known by the name Saṅkarṣaṇa, in the form of self-concentration, Bhava approaches Him while reciting this hymn. The Blessed Lord said:

"Oṃ, obeisances unto the Blessed One, the Great Person, the source of all qualities, the infinite, the unmanifest; obeisances! I worship You, whose lotus feet are the refuge for those who seek shelter—the supreme goal of all that is auspicious; You who, out of Your affection for devotees, manifest Yourself as the creator of all beings; the Lord who removes worldly existence and is the very essence of being."
The vision of one who beholds Him is not tainted even in the slightest degree by the fluctuations of the mind caused by His illusory energies;
for how could anyone who desires to conquer his own self not revere that Lord, whose impetuous wrath is unconquerable?
He appears through His illusory power as if unreal to those of perverted vision, like a man with eyes reddened by honeyed liquor appearing intoxicated.
The wives of the Nāgas were not even able to offer worship out of shame, for their senses had been overwhelmed by the touch of his feet.
The sages call him the one who is devoid of the three states—sustenance, birth, and dissolution—and who is infinite;
they do not perceive him standing anywhere on the circle of the earth, which is like a mere trifle, within the abodes of his thousand heads.
From whom, it is said, there arose today the unborn Lord Mahān, whose form consists of the modes and who is the abode of pure consciousness;
from whose birth I, by my own threefold power, create the modes of goodness, darkness, and the senses. We all remain under the control of that Great Soul, like birds bound by a string.

O Great One, we—the ego, the intellect, the modes of passion and ignorance, and the senses—all create this universe by Your grace. To You, whose nature is both dissolution and emergence, I offer my obeisances; for this person, deluded by the creation of the material qualities, does not easily know the means of deliverance from the illusory power (māyā) fashioned by You, which consists of the stages of karma.
Śrī Śuka said:

And likewise, O King, there was one named Bhadraśravas, the son of Dharma; the men who were the lords of that family in the region of Bhadrāśva worshipped with supreme devotion the beloved form of the Lord Vāsudeva, which consists of dharma and is known as Hayaśīrṣa.
Bringing [the Lord] near through meditative concentration and reciting this, they approached Him;
the sons of Bhadraśravas said:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Dharma; obeisance to the purifier of the self."

Oh, how wonderful is the Lord’s inscrutable activity! While He destroys, people look on with indifference and do not see; when they contemplate the unreal and practice forbidden acts, they even wish to live by killing their own sons and fathers.
Wise sages declare the universe to be perishable, and the learned who know the supreme self perceive it as such.
Nevertheless, O Unborn One, they are deluded by Your Māyā; I bow down to You, whose work is most wonderful and who Yourself remain unborn.

Indeed, the acts of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe are attributed to You, though You are the non-agent; yet You remain unattached. This is not surprising in You, who are both the effect and the cause, the Self of all, and yet in reality distinct from them.

"To Him who, at the end of the age, assumed the form of a man and a horse and recovered the Vedas that had been obscured by darkness from the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the sake of the sage who petitioned Him—to You, whose activities are never in vain, I offer my obeisances.
And in Harivarṣa, the Blessed Lord likewise resides in the form of Nara-Hari; the purpose for assuming that form is as follows:

I shall describe that beloved form later on. Prahlāda—the highly fortunate one who is a vessel for the qualities of a Great Person (mahā-puruṣa), whose nature and conduct sanctify the lineages of the Daityas and Dānavas—worships Him together with the inhabitants of that realm through an uninterrupted yoga of exclusive devotion, and he recites this:
"Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed One, Narasiṃha; obeisances to the splendor of splendors! Manifest, manifest! (BhP 5.18.8).
O Vajra-clawed one, O Vajra-fanged one, destroy, destroy the latent impressions of karma; swallow, swallow the darkness! Oṃ svāhā!
May fearlessness be abundant within me, Oṃ kṣraum!
May there be well-being for the universe; may the wicked be appeased; and may all beings meditate upon each other with auspicious intent.
May our minds be auspiciously absorbed in Adhokṣaja, and may our intellect be fixed upon Him without any ulterior motive.
May we have no attachment to home, wife, children, wealth, or kinsmen, but rather toward those who are dear to the Blessed Lord.
One who is self-possessed and satisfied with the mere maintenance of life attains perfection before long; such is not the case for one who is a slave to the senses.
The mind of those who repeatedly touch that sacred ford—which has acquired its own majestic power through association with Him—purifies the heart of the Unborn One;
for when He is reached through the Vedas, He removes even the god of love. Who indeed would not serve the prowess of Mukunda?
In whomsoever there is unselfish devotion to the Blessed Lord, in him all the gods abide through their various qualities.
For one who is not a devotee of Hari, how can there be great qualities? One runs outward after that which is unreal through the power of mere desire.
Indeed, Lord Hari is the manifest Supreme Person and the Self of all embodied beings, just as water is the desired object for fish.
If, having abandoned Him, one becomes attached to the home, then the "greatness" of such householders consists merely in their age.

"Therefore, having abandoned the home— which is the root of passion, attachment, despondency, anger, pride, longing, fear, and wretchedness, and which is the entire cycle of worldly existence— worship the feet of Nṛsiṃha, who is free from all fear.
In Ketumāla as well, the Blessed One, in the form of Kāmadeva, acted out of a desire to please Lakṣmī.
The embryos of Prajāpati’s daughters— whose numbers equal the days and nights of a human lifespan and who are the presiding deities of those respective years—
perish at the end of the year, their lives destroyed as their minds are agitated by the splendor of the Great Person’s great weapons.
This occurs through the playful charm of His exceedingly graceful gait, amorous gestures, and the playfulness of His beautiful smiles and glances.
Delighting Ramā with the beauty of his lotus-face, made charming by slightly raised and beautiful arched brows, he delights the senses.

That form of the Blessed One, composed of *māyā*, the goddess Ramā worships through supreme meditative yoga (*parama-samādhi-yoga*) during the nights of the year, accompanied by the daughters of Prajāpati, and during the days, accompanied by their husbands;
she recites this [verse]:
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ oṃ, obeisances unto the Blessed One, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose self is distinguished by all specific qualities;

the sovereign lord of intentions, thoughts, consciousnesses, and particularities; who consists of the sixteen digits, who is composed of the Vedic meters, who is composed of food, who is composed of nectar, and who is composed of everything; obeisances to the one who is power, vigor, strength, and splendor; obeisances to the one who is desire and the object of desire; may there be obeisance unto You in both states.

Women, having worshipped you, Hṛṣīkeśvara, by means of vows, naturally desire another husband in this world. Yet, since they are not independent, you do not protect their children, their dear ones, their wealth, or their lives. He alone is a true husband who himself protects his people from fear on all sides, being free from fear himself.
He is indeed one alone; otherwise, he would not consider anything other than the attainment of his own self to be a source of fear.
O Blessed One, she who desires the worship of Your lotus feet is greedy for all worldly desires;
yet it is that very worship which is her true desire, for she suffers when her prayer is rejected. She is the one truly desired and honored by You.

O Unconquered One, for the sake of attaining Me, the gods, lords, asuras, and others perform fierce austerities with their minds fixed on Indra; yet, apart from those who are devoted to Your feet, they do not find Me, because I am held within Your heart. Therefore, O Acyuta, You whose lotus hand was placed upon the heads of the Sātvatas—those very hands are now honored by me upon my own head.
"O most excellent one, you bear me as your mark by your divine power (*māyā*); for who is capable of fathoming the purposeful will of the Lord?

And in the realm of Ramyaka, he worships even now with great yoga of devotion that form of the Blessed One’s most beloved Matsya incarnation, which was previously manifested to Manu, the lord of that region.

He offers this prayer: "Om, obeisances to the Blessed One, the foremost of all; obeisances to the essence of goodness (*sattva*), to the vital breath, to vigor, to endurance, to strength—to the Great Fish."
With a form unseen by all the guardians of the worlds, you wander both within and without, possessing a mighty voice;
you are that Lord who has brought this universe under His control by Your name, just as a man brings a wooden puppet under his command.
Indeed, the world-protectors, afflicted by the fever of envy, have abandoned You even while striving to reach You, both individually and collectively.
Neither bipeds nor quadrupeds, nor any crawling creature, nor anything stationary that is seen here, were able to drink [the waters].

O Unborn One, You traverse this earth—the repository of herbs and creepers—along with me by Your power, as if it were a wave-crowned ocean at the end of a Yuga; obeisance to You, the Self of the multitude of life-breaths of the universe.

The Blessed One also dwells within the golden [egg], assuming the form of a tortoise; Aryaman, the lord of the host of ancestors, together with the persons of that region, approaches His most beloved form and recites this mantra:

"Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed One, the Tortoise, who is distinguished by all the qualities of living beings, whose station is unperceived; obeisances to the Supreme Body, obeisances to the Infinite, obeisances, obeisances to the Abode."
Obeisances to You!
This form of Yours, presented by Your own *māyā*, is the very nature of reality yet manifested in many forms;
since it has no fixed number because it is perceived in ways that do not correspond [to its true nature], obeisances to You whose form is indefinable.
The womb-born, the sweat-born, the egg-born, and the soil-born; the moving and the non-moving; the gods, sages, ancestors, and elemental beings; the senses;
heaven, ether, earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, islands, planets, and constellations—all these are designated as the one [Supreme Being].
Within Him, whose names, forms, and appearances are innumerable, this world has been conceived by the wise.
"Salutations to You, the teacher of Sāṅkhya, by whose vision of reality [the world] is removed through enumeration.
And in the northern Kurus, the Blessed Lord, the Person of Sacrifice, remains in the form of the performed Boar;
to Him this Goddess Earth, together with the Kurus, approaches with unswerving yoga of devotion, and to this supreme [teaching].
He recites the Upaniṣad:

"Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed One, whose true nature is the mark of the mantras, who is the sacrifice and the ritual, the constituent part of the great sacrificial rite; obeisances to the Great Person, who is purified by action, who appears in the three ages.
Obeisances to Him whose true form the wise and learned perceive within the modes of nature, just as they perceive fire within pieces of wood."
Salutations again and again to Him whose true nature is sought by those desiring to see the hidden reality through the churning-stick of the mind, using the means of ritual action;
to Him whose essence is perceived as the Reality through the qualities of Māyā—consisting of substance, action, cause, the path, the lord, and the agent;
and to Him who has cast aside all that is fashioned by Māyā through the investigation of the self, which transcends the limbs of the body and the intellect.

Salutations to You, the witness of qualities and actions, whose will alone brings about the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, yet who remains untouched by the modes of nature; for whom the illusory energy (māyā) revolves as its support like a wheel on an axle, though he is not moved by it; salutations to that primordial Boar who, having crushed the Daitya Prativāraṇa in battle, rescued me from the netherworld (rasātala).
Having placed his fore-tusks [upon the mountain], he emerged from the ocean like a sporting elephant; "I bow down to that all-pervading Lord," thus [he spoke].
Śrī Śuka said:
In the region of Kimpuruṣa, [one should meditate upon] the Blessed One, the Original Person, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, who is delightful to Sītā.
The supreme devotee Hanumān, delighting in the proximity of Rāma’s feet and possessing unceasing devotion, attends upon Him along with the Kiṃpuruṣas.
Together with the Gandharvas, he listens to the most auspicious narrations concerning his lord, the Blessed One, as they are sung by Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and he himself sings this:
Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed One of excellent renown; obeisances to Him whose character, conduct, and vows are those of the noble ones.

Salutations to the one who has trained himself and served the world; salutations to the touchstone for the praise of the virtuous; salutations to the god who is devoted to Brahman, the Great Person, the Great King. That which is the one, pure experience alone, by its own splendor having destroyed the arrangement of the modes [of nature]—*BhP 5.19.4*.
I take refuge in that which is inward-turned, perfectly tranquil, perceivable only by the wise, devoid of name and form, and free from the sense of "I.
The descent of the Lord into mortal form here was for the instruction of mortals and for the slaying of demons; it was certainly not for His own sake.
Otherwise, how could there be such sufferings caused by Sītā for the Sovereign who delights in His own Self?
Indeed, that Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the best friend of those who possess self-mastery, is not attached to the three worlds;
He would never succumb to the distress caused by women, nor would He ever abandon Lakṣmaṇa.
Surely neither birth, nor greatness, nor good fortune, nor speech, nor intellect, nor form is a cause for His satisfaction.
"Alas, even though we were forest-dwellers released by them, Lakṣmaṇa’s elder brother made us his friends!

Whether he be a god, an asura, a monkey, or a human, whoever with all their heart worships Rāma— the supreme Hari who knows how to repay kindness and who led the people of Kosala to the northern heaven— [attains the highest goal]."

In the land of Bhārata as well, the Blessed One known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa performs austerity with an unmanifested gait out of compassion for the sake of favoring those who possess self-control, until the end of the kalpa, so that they may attain the realization of the Self characterized by dharma, knowledge, detachment, sovereignty, tranquility, and cessation.
The Blessed Lord Nārada [instructs] those people of Bhārata, who abide by the system of social classes and stages of life, by means of the two [scriptures] proclaimed by the Blessed One...
Having described the power of the Blessed One through Sāṅkhya and Yoga, Sāvarṇi approaches Him with a state of supreme devotion as he is about to receive instruction, and recites this prayer:

"Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed One, whose nature is tranquility, who has ceased from the sense of self; obeisances to Him whose only wealth is His lack of possessions, the bull among sages, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme teacher of the paramahaṃsas, the sovereign Lord who delights in the Self—obeisances, obeisances!"* *Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.19.11* *Note: The original Sanskrit text contains the phrase "paramahaṃsa-parama-gurave," which is translated here as "the supreme teacher of the paramahaṃsas."*
And he sings this:
"Salutations to Him who is the agent in the creation and other processes of this world, yet is not bound nor slain even though situated within the body by bodily afflictions;
whose vision as the Seer is never defiled by the modes of nature—to that unattached, discerning Witness, I bow."
For this indeed is the skill in yoga taught by the Blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, O Lord of Yoga:
that at the time of death, one who has cast off the wretched body should fix the mind with devotion upon You, who are beyond the modes of nature;
whereas one who is greedy for desires in this world and the next remains preoccupied with children, wives, and wealth.
The wise man who fears the passing away of this wretched body exerts himself in vain; it is merely labor.

Therefore, O Lord Adhokṣaja, grant us that yoga which is by nature directed toward You, so that we may quickly shatter this "I" and "mine" attached to the wretched body through Your māyā—a state that is otherwise very difficult to break. Thus we pray.
In this land of Bhārata-varṣa, there are also many rivers and mountains: Malaya, Maṅgalaprastha,
Maināka, Trikūṭa, Ṛṣabha, Kūṭaka, Kollaka, Sahya, Devagiri, Ṛṣyamūka, Śrīśaila, Veṅkaṭa,
Mahendra, Vāridhāra, Vindhya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣagiri, Pāriyātra, Droṇa, Citrakūṭa, and Govardhana.

There are Raivataka, Kakubha, Nīla, Gokāmukha, Indrakīla, Kāmagiri, and hundreds of thousands of other mountains; from their slopes flow innumerable rivers and streams. The people of Bhārata purify themselves by touching with their own bodies the waters of these [rivers], which purify by their very names.
The Candravasā, Tāmraparṇī, Avaṭodā, Kṛtamālā, Vaihāyasī, Kāverī, Veṇī, Payasvinī,
Śarkarāvartā, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kṛṣṇāveṇyā, Bhīmarathī, Godāvarī, Nirvindhyā, Payoṣṇī, Tāpī, Revā,
Surasā, Narmadā, Carmaṇvatī, Sindhu, Andha, and Śoṇa— these are the rivers; as well as the Mahānadī, Vedasmṛti, and Ṛṣikulyā.
The Trisāmā, Kauśikī, Mandākinī, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Dṛṣadvatī, Gomatī, Sarayū, Rodhasvatī, Saptavatī,
Suṣomā, Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Asiknī, and Viśvā— these are the great rivers.
(BhP 5.19.19) In this very land, those who have obtained birth among men [are distinguished] by their fair, red, or dark complexions.

By their own commenced karma, many divine, human, and hellish destinies are indeed ordained for all beings in succession, according to the regulations of their respective castes; and liberation also occurs for those who [take refuge] in that Blessed One, the Supreme Self, who is the self of all beings, who is without a body, indefinable, and without abode. (BhP 5.19.20)

When there is association with the Supreme Person through the yoga of devotion characterized by having no other motive directed toward Vāsudeva—by means of which the knot of ignorance that causes various states of existence is severed—it is precisely this that the gods sing of: *“O Great-souled One, we have come to You for refuge; please deliver us from this ocean of worldly existence.”* (BhP 5.19.21)

"Aha! What auspicious deed have these men performed, or has Hari himself become gracious toward them, that they have obtained birth among men in the field of Bhārata, which is conducive to the service of Mukunda? For such is our own longing.
Of what use to us are difficult sacrifices, austerities, vows, gifts, and the like, or the fruitless conquest of heaven?"

Where the remembrance of the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa is not lost despite the excessive festival of the senses, even for those with a lifespan of a kalpa— though they may attain such a station, it is better to have a life of but a moment on the land of Bhārata. For by a single moment as a mortal, a wise person, having renounced everything, attains the fearless abode of Hari.
That world where the nectar-river of stories concerning Vaikuṇṭha does not flow, where there are no saintly devotees who take refuge in Him,
and where there are no great festivals of sacrifices to the Lord of Sacrifice— that realm of the lords of the gods is certainly not to be sought after.
But those beings who have attained a human birth here, which is equipped with the full array of knowledge, action, and material resources, [should utilize it for the service of the Lord].
Those who do not strive for the state beyond rebirth will surely fall again into bondage, like forest-dwellers returning to their snares.
Yet, by those who have offered oblations on the sacrificial grass according to the prescribed rules, mantras, and substances, with faith and devotion—
oblations which are the portions of the One who is invoked under various names— the Lord, being Himself full, joyfully accepts them and grants the fulfillment of all blessings.

It is true that when entreated by men, he grants their requested object; yet he does not grant it simply because it was requested, since he himself bestows his own sprout-like feet upon those who worship him, even if they desire nothing else—thereby concealing all other desires.
Whatever merit remains for us here from our well-offered oblations, our hymns, and our good deeds, [may it lead us to you].
"By that merit, may we have a birth endowed with mindfulness in the realm of Ajanābha, where Lord Hari bestows auspiciousness upon those who worship Him.
Śrī Śuka said:

O King, some teachers point out eight subcontinents (*upadvīpas*) of Jambūdvīpa, which were established by the sons of Sagara while they were digging up this earth on all sides in search of the horse.
They are as follows: Svarṇaprastha, Candraśukla, Āvartana, Ramaṇaka, Mandarahariṇa, Pāñcajanya, Siṃhala, and Laṅkā.
Thus, O best of the Bharatas, the division of the regions of Jambūdvīpa has been described to you according to the traditional instruction.
Śrī Śuka said:
From this point forward, the division of the regions (varṣas) according to their dimensions, characteristics, and configurations, beginning with Plakṣa and the others, will be described.
This Jambūdvīpa, which has a certain extent of width, is surrounded by the salt ocean (kṣārodadhi) of equal extent;
just as Mount Meru is surrounded by the one called Jambu, so too is the salt ocean surrounded by the region called Plakṣa, which is twice as wide as it.
Just as there is a moat surrounded by an outer grove, so too has there arisen a golden mountain named after the continent, equal in size to a jambū tree,

where the seven-tongued fire resides; its sovereign was Idhmajihva, the son of Priyavrata, who, having divided his own continent into seven regions and assigned them to his sons according to those seven regional names, retired from worldly affairs through the yoga of self-realization.

Śiva, Yavasa, Subhadra, Śānta, Kṣema, Amṛta, and Abhaya—these are the seven regions. Within them, seven mountains and seven rivers are well known: Maṇikūṭa, Vajrakūṭa, Indrasena, Jyotiṣmat, Suparṇa, Hiraṇyaṣṭhīva, and Meghamāla are the boundary mountains; Aruṇā, Nṛmṇā, Aṅgirasī, Sāvitrī, Suptabhātā, Ṛtambharā, and Satyambharā are the great rivers.

By the mere touch of whose waters the four castes— their dust and darkness shaken off— were known by the names Haṃsa, Pataṅga, Ūrdhvāyana, and Satyāṅga; they lived for a thousand years, possessed appearances and progeny like those of the gods, and through the triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā) worshipped the Blessed One, the Sun, who consists of the three Vedas, as their own Self at the gateway to heaven.
"O ancient Viṣṇu, we pray to the Sun, the Self, who is the form of truth, of cosmic order, of Brahman,
of immortality, and of death.

In the five regions beginning with Plakṣa, the natural perfection of all men— consisting of longevity, sensory power, vitality, endurance, strength, intelligence, and prowess— exists without distinction.

Just as the Plakṣa continent is surrounded by the Ikṣurasoda ocean of equal extent, so too the Śālmala continent, twice as large, is encompassed by the Suroda ocean of equal extent. Therein indeed stands a Śālmali tree, equal in height to the Plakṣa, which is said to be the abode of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) when he is praised with Vedic hymns; that tree serves as the distinguishing mark for the name of the continent. The lord of that continent was Yajñabāhu, the son of Priyavrata, who [divided it] among his seven sons.
He divided those seven regions according to their names: Surocana, Saumanasya, Ramaṇaka, Devavarṣa, Pāribhadra, Āpyāyana, and Avijñāta (BhP 5.20.10).
In those regions, seven mountain ranges and rivers are well known: Svarasa, Śataśṛṅga, Vāmadeva, and so forth.
Kunda, Mukunda, Puṣpavarṣa, Sahasraśruti, Anumati, Sinīvālī, Sarasvatī, Kuhū, Rajanī, Nandā, and Rākā— these are the names of the personified deities of those regions (BhP 5.20.11).
The inhabitants of those regions, known as Śrutadharas, Vīryadharas, Vasundharas, and Īṣandharas, worship the Lord Soma, who consists of the Vedas and is their own self, with the Vedas (BhP 5.20.12),
distributing him among the ancestors and the gods through their own rays during the dark and light fortnights.
"May Soma be the king of all our subjects.
Thus, outside the Suroda ocean lies Kuśadvīpa, twice its size and surrounded by an ocean of clarified butter (Ghṛtoda) equal to itself, just as the former was.
In that island stands a clump of Kuśa grass created by the gods, which gives the island its name; like another blazing fire, it illuminates the quarters with the luster of its own shoots.

O King, the lord of that continent, the son of Priyavrata named Hiraṇyaretas, having divided his own continent into seven portions for his seven sons— namely Vasu, Vasudāna, Dṛḍharuci, Nābhigupta, Stutyavrata, Vivikta, and Vāmadeva— himself devoted himself to ascetic penance.
In their respective regions, there are seven well-known boundary mountains and seven rivers each, known as Cakro.
The rivers are Catuḥśṛṅgā, Kapilā, Citrakūṭā, Devānīkā, Ūrdhvaromā, Draviṇā, Rasakulyā, Madhukulyā,
Mitravindā, Śrutavindā, Devagarbhā, Ghṛtacyutā, and Mantramālā (BhP 5.20.16).
With their waters, the inhabitants of Kuśadvīpa— known as the Kuśalas, Kovidas, Abhiyuktas, and Kulakas— worship the Blessed One in the form of Jātavedas through their skill in ritual action.
"O Jātavedas, you are the direct bearer of oblations for the Supreme Brahman;
through sacrifice, worship the Puruṣa who is the constituent limb of the gods.
Thus, beyond the Ocean of Clarified Butter is Krauñcadvīpa, which is twice as large as itself, surrounded by the Ocean of Milk.
Kuśadvīpa is surrounded and encircled by the ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtoda), just as it was described. In that island dwells the king of mountains named Krauñca, which gives the island its name.
Although the mountain’s slopes and groves were once shattered by the weapons of Guha, it has now become free from fear, being sprinkled by the Ocean of Milk and protected by the Lord Varuṇa.
In that island also, the son of Priyavrata named Ghṛtapṛṣṭha was the sovereign, [dividing] his own island into regions (varṣas).

Having divided those seven sons who bore the name "Putra" and established seven heirs as rulers over the regions, the Blessed One himself approached the lotus feet of Lord Hari—the source of his own being, whose fame is supremely auspicious. [The seven were:
Āma, Madhurūha, Meghapṛṣṭha, Sudhāmā, Bhrājiṣṭha, Lohitārṇa, and Vanaspati.

Thus, the sons of Ghṛtapṛṣṭha are those seven mountain ranges of the Varṣa, and seven rivers are likewise renowned: Śuklā, Vardhamānā, Bhojanā, Upabarhiṇī, Nandā, Nandanā, and Sarvatobhadrā; and [the rivers] Abhayā, Amṛtaughā, Āryakā, Tīrthavatī, Rūpavatī, Pavitravatī, and Śuklā.

"O Bull among Men, those inhabitants of the regions known as Puruṣa, Ṛṣabha, Draviṇa, and Devaka, who partake of their pure and stainless waters, offer a full handful of water to the Lord composed of water with the mantra:
'O Waters, you possess the potency of the Supreme Person; purifying the earth, the mid-region, and heaven—may you, the destroyers of sin, purify us; may you touch us with your essence, O Earth!'"

Thus, Śākadvīpa is situated all around Kṣīroda to the east; it is thirty-two hundred thousand yojanas in extent and is surrounded by an ocean of equal size consisting of curd-cream (dadhi-maṇḍoda). In that island stands a great tree named Śāka, which gives its name to the region and whose exceedingly fragrant scent perfumes the entire island.
The sovereign of that region was Medhātithi, the son of Priyavrata; he too,
having divided the seven regions and named them after his sons— Purojava, Manojava, Pavamāna, Dhūmrānīka, Citrarepha, Bahurūpa, and Viśvadhāra—
appointed those sons as their respective rulers and, with his mind absorbed in the Blessed Lord Ananta, entered the forest of asceticism.

The boundary mountains and rivers of these regions are likewise seven each: the mountains are Īśāna, Uruśṛṅga, Balabhadra, Śatakesara, Sahasrasrotas, Devapāla, and Mahānasa; and the rivers are Anaghā, Āyurdā, Ubhayaspṛṣṭi, Aparājitā, Pañcapadī, Sahasrasruti, and Nijadhṛti.

The inhabitants of that region— named Ṛtavrata, Satyavrata, Dānavrata, and Anuvrata— having shaken off the qualities of passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas) through breath control (prāṇāyāma), enter within by means of supreme meditative absorption (parama-samādhi) and worship the Blessed One whose nature is air (vāyu). "May the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), the Lord, who directly sustains all beings by His own manifestations, and who is clearly under whose control [all things] exist, protect us."
In this very manner, beyond the ocean of curd-cream (dadhi-maṇḍoda) is Puṣkaradvīpa, twice as extensive in circumference;

it is surrounded on the outside by an ocean of sweet water (svādūdaka) of equal extent, within which is fashioned a great lotus with tens of millions upon tens of millions of petals of pure, blazing gold, serving as the seat for the Lord Kamalāsana.

In the center of that island stands a single mountain named Mānasottara, which serves as the boundary between the inner and outer regions; it is ten thousand *yojanas* in height and breadth. Upon it are the four cities of the world-protectors, Indra and the others, above which is the wheel of the sun’s chariot that revolves around Meru, constituting the year.
It revolves by means of the days and nights of the gods.

The sovereign of that island is Vītihotra, the son of Priyavrata; having appointed his two sons, named Ramaṇaka and Dhātaki, as the lords of the regions, he himself, like his predecessors, is devoted to the service of the Lord. The people of that region worship the Lord in the form of Brahmā through ritual action, and they recite this:
Whatever sign composed of action a person may worship as the sign of Brahman— saying, "Obeisance to that Blessed Lord, who is solitary, non-dual, and peaceful"—
beyond that lies the mountain named Lokāloka, situated all around in the interval between the worlds of light and darkness.
The distance between Mānasottara and Meru is equal to the extent of another golden land, which is like the surface of a mirror;
because any object placed upon it can never again be perceived, that land was avoided by all living beings.
It is known as Lokāloka, for by this mountain, the boundary between the worlds (loka) and the non-worlds (aloka) is established.

That [egg] was fashioned all around by the Lord at the edge of the three worlds; for the rays of the hosts of luminaries, from the sun to Dhruva, which extend downwards through the three worlds, are never able to turn back upwards as far as its binding circumference.

This much is the arrangement of the world, conceived by the wise through its measurements, characteristics, and configurations; yet this [known world] is but a fourth part of the terrestrial globe calculated at fifty crores of yojanas. Above it, in the four directions, the Self-born One, the Teacher of the Entire World, has stationed the lords of elephants—Ṛṣabha, Puṣkaracūḍa, Vāmana, and Aparājita—who are the causes for the stability of all the worlds.

To augment the various powers of those world-protectors who are His own manifestations, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Great Person and Master of Great Opulence, acting as the inner controller, surrounded by His foremost attendants such as Viṣvaksena, and adorned with His own staff-like arms bearing His characteristic weapons, manifested His own pure essence characterized by the eight great perfections beginning with virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.

Maintaining [the mountain], he remains on that best of mountains for the welfare of the entire world until the end of the kalpa; this is the meaning: the Blessed One has assumed such an appearance through his own power of yoga-māyā for the sake of protecting the various worldly activities fashioned by it.
By this internal extent, the measurement of the non-world (aloka) is also explained—that which lies beyond the Lokāloka mountain; they describe that as the pure realm of the Lord of Yoga.

Situated within the cosmic egg, the sun is that which lies between heaven and earth; between the solar orb and the shell of the egg, there are twenty-five crores [of yojanas]. When this egg perished, he who was therein became known as Mārtaṇḍa because of his origin from the golden egg (mṛt-aṇḍa); and he is called Hiraṇyagarbha because of his birth from the golden egg (hiraṇya-aṇḍa).
For by the sun indeed are distinguished the directions, the atmosphere, the heavens, and the earth;
as well as heaven and liberation, the hells, and all the abodes of the waters;
and [the distinctions between] gods, animals, humans, reptiles, and plants.
The sun is the self, the eye, and the lord of all classes of living beings.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus far has the configuration of the terrestrial sphere been explained according to its measurements and characteristics.

By this [measurement], those who know it teach the measurement of the orb of heaven; just as there is space between two halves of a split pea or similar seed, so too is the intermediate space (antarikṣa) situated between those two, joined at their junction.

Within that middle space is the Blessed Lord, the Lord of Heat, the Sun, who heats the three worlds with his heat and illuminates them with his own radiance. He is known by the names *udagayana*, *dakṣiṇāyana*, and *vaiṣuvata*.

Moving with slow, swift, or moderate speeds during his ascent, descent, and stationing at equal points according to the seasons, he ordains days and nights as long, short, or equal within the zodiacal signs beginning with Capricorn.
When he moves through Aries and Libra, the days and nights become equal. When...
When [the sun] moves through the five zodiac signs beginning with Taurus, then the days increase and the nights decrease by one *ghaṭikā* each month;
when it resides in the five signs beginning with Scorpio, then the days and nights become the reverse.
As long as it is the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), the days increase; as long as it is the northern course (udagayana), the nights increase.
Thus, they teach that the circumference of the Mānasottara mountain is ninety-five million one hundred thousand (*95,100,000*) *yojanas*.
On that mountain, to the east of Meru is Indra’s city named Devadhānī, and to the south is Yama’s city, Saṃyamanī.

To the west is the river named Vāruṇī, to the north is the Saumyā named Vibhāvarī; these are the causes for the activity and cessation of beings at sunrise, midday, sunset, and midnight respectively, according to the specific times around the four directions of Meru. For those residing there, the sun always shines directly overhead at midday, moving to the left of the mountain with its northern course and to the right with its southern course.

Wherever it rises, at the same meridian line it sets; wherever it shines with its radiance, at that same meridian line it causes sleep. Those who might perceive it do not see it once it has gone there.
And when it moves from the city of Indra, in fifteen *ghaṭikās* it travels two and a quarter crores and twelve and a half lakhs of *yojanas*, plus a little more, toward the city of Yama.
Thus, from there, the western, northern, and eastern [directions] as well as other planets such as the Moon, together with the constellations, rise in the circle of luminaries;
or else, in this manner, within a single *muhūrta*, the solar chariot—which consists of the three Vedas and measures thirty-four lakh and eight hundred *yojanas*—revolves through the four cities.
Its single wheel has twelve spokes, six rims, and three naves, and its nature is that of the year.

They declare that its axle is fixed upon the summit of Meru; one half of it is placed on Mānasottara, where the wheel of the sun’s chariot is mounted. Revolving like the wheel of an oil-press, it revolves around Mount Mānasottara.
Upon that axle, a second axle is fixed at its base, measuring a quarter of the length, with its upper portion fixed upon the Dhruva pole, like the axle of an oil-press.

The interior of the chariot is thirty-six lakṣa yojanas long and one-fourth of that in width; the yoke of the sun’s chariot is of the same measure, where seven horses named after the Vedic meters, yoked by Aruṇa, carry the divine Āditya.
It is said that Aruṇa stands before the Sun and is likewise appointed to the task of driving behind him.
Likewise, sixty thousand Vālakhilya sages, each the size of a thumb-joint, stationed in front of the sun, offer praise with hymns of praise (*sūkta-vāka*) as they are appointed to do so.
Similarly, other groups— consisting of sages, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Grāmaṇīs, Yātudhānas, and Devas,
numbering seven and fourteen respectively— worship the Blessed Sun, who is their own self, month by month under various names.
Having distinct and various names, they worship [the sun] in pairs through their separate activities.
The King said:
"Regarding this [movement] of the divine Sun as he circumambulates Meru and Dhruva from left to right..."
"How shall we understand that which the Blessed One has described as moving toward the zodiac signs and being counter-clockwise?
He replied:
"Just as when a potter's wheel is spinning, the ants and other creatures resting upon it also spin along with it."

The motion is indeed different because it is perceived even in other locations; likewise, the motion of the planets such as the Sun and others— which revolve along with the wheel of time marked by the constellations and zodiac signs as they circumambulate the Pole Star and Mount Meru to the right— is distinct, because it is perceived within different constellations and different zodiac signs.

This very Lord, the Original Person, Nārāyaṇa himself, for the welfare of the worlds, divides Himself— who consists of the three Vedas— into twelve parts as a means for the purification of ritual action; thus, even by the wise through the Veda, He is sought to be known as He ordains the seasonal qualities according to their respective inclinations during the six seasons beginning with spring.

In this world, those persons who follow the conduct of their respective social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), worshiping Him with faith through the threefold Vedic knowledge, through various prescribed rituals— both high and low— and through elaborate yogic practices,
attain the highest good directly.
Furthermore, He is that very Self who exists within the worlds between heaven and earth, in the sphere of the sky.

The Kālacakra, having entered [the zodiac], consumes the twelve months known as the signs (*rāśi*), which are the constituents of the year; a month is taught to consist of two fortnights, namely day and night, together with two and a half constellations (*nakṣatra*). That period by which one would consume a sixth part [of the year] is indeed taught as a season (*ṛtu*), a constituent of the year.
Moreover, the time during which it traverses half the celestial path is called an *ayana*.

Furthermore, the time during which it completely occupies the entire circle of the sky along with the circles of heaven and earth is known as a *saṃvatsara*, a *parivatsara*, an *iḍāvatsara*, an *anuvatsara*, or simply a *vatsara*.
Thus they declare the slow, fast, and equal motions of the sun.
In this way, the moon, being perceived one hundred thousand yojanas above the rays of the sun,
traverses the sun's annual course in two fortnights, its monthly course with one and a half lunar mansions (nakṣatras), and its fortnightly course in a single day.
Moving as the foremost, he traverses more swiftly;

by means of the lunar digits being filled for the immortals and the digits waning for the ancestors, he extends the days and nights through the bright and dark fortnights, serving as the vital breath for the multitude of all living beings.
And the individual soul (*jīva*) traverses one single lunar mansion in thirty *muhūrtas*.

This person (*puruṣa*), who consists of sixteen parts, is the Blessed One composed of mind and composed of food; because he is the life-breath (*prāṇa*) for gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, cattle, birds, reptiles, and plants, and because his nature is to be the refuge (*āyana*) of all, they describe him as "consisting of all" (*sarvamaya*).

Two hundred thousand yojanas above that, to the south of Meru, are the constellations—twenty-eight in number, including Abhijit—impelled by the Lord through the medium of Time (Kālāyana). Two hundred thousand yojanas further above that is found Uśanas; he moves like the sun, sometimes ahead, sometimes behind, or alongside it, with a speed, slowness, or equality of motion identical to the sun's, always acting for the benefit of the worlds.
Thus, by its movement, it is generally inferred to pacify the obstruction of rain and the malefic planets.

Budha was described by Uśanas; beyond that, at a distance of two hundred thousand *yojanas*, the son of Soma (Budha) is perceived. Generally bringing auspiciousness, when he deviates from the Sun, one anticipates fear of excessive winds, clouds, drought, and the like.
Above that, at a distance of two hundred thousand *yojanas*, the planet Aṅgāraka (Mars) is perceived;

he traverses each of the twelve zodiac signs one by one in three fortnights each, provided he does not move in retrograde motion—for he is generally an inauspicious planet, a herald of calamity. Above that, at an interval of two hundred thousand *yojanas*, the venerable Bṛhaspati moves through each zodiac sign for a full year (*parivatsara*), provided he is not retrograde.
He is generally favorable toward the community of Brahmins.

Above that, at a distance of two hundred thousand yojanas, Saturn (Śanaiścara) is perceived; moving slowly, he lingers for thirty months in each zodiac sign and thus revolves through all of them over as many years, generally being favorable.
Indeed, he causes unrest for all;
beyond that, at a distance of eleven hundred thousand yojanas, the sages are found who, bringing peace to the worlds, circumambulate the supreme abode of the Blessed Viṣṇu.
Śrī Śuka said: Now,

beyond that, at a distance of thirteen hundred thousand *yojanas*, is that which they call the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, where the great devotee Dhruva, son of Uttānapāda, [was established] by Agni and Indra.

Being honored with great respect by Prajāpati Kaśyapa, by Dharma, and by those of his own time, he now remains as a source of livelihood for those who live for a kalpa; thus has his majesty been described here.

For he is the fixed support for all the hosts of luminaries—the planets, constellations, and so forth—as they are whirled about by the Lord Time, who is unblinking and possesses unmanifest speed. He stands like a pillar.
Ordained by the Lord, it shines eternally;
