just as sacrificial animals bound to the central pillar move in circles according to their respective places through the three daily libations, so too do the constellations, planets, and other celestial bodies move within this sphere through an internal and external conjunction.
Fixed upon the axle of Time and impelled by the wind, they traverse the sky until the end of the kalpa,
like clouds or hawks driven by the wind; even so, these hosts of luminaries,
supported by the union of Prakṛti and Puruṣa and having their courses fashioned by karma, do not fall to the earth.

Some describe this host of lights in the form of a *śiśumāra* (porpoise) for the purpose of meditative concentration (*yoga-dhāraṇā*) upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. At the tip of its tail, which is turned downward with its body coiled, Dhruva is situated;
on its tail are Prajāpati, Agni, Indra, and Dharma; and at the base of the tail are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, while Kaṭyā is located on its waist.

The seven Ṛṣis [are situated] on the right flank of his body, which is coiled in a clockwise direction; they arrange the constellations of the northern course (udagayana) upon his right side, while those of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) are on the left. Just as the limbs on both sides of a porpoise coiled in a circular form are equal in number, so too are the Ajavīthī on its back and the celestial Gaṅgā on its belly.

The two *punarvasu* and *puṣya* [nakṣatras] are on the right and left hips; *ārdrā* and *aśleṣā* are on the right and left hind feet; *abhijit* and *uttarāṣāḍhā* are on the right and left nostrils respectively; *śravaṇa* and *pūrvāṣāḍhā* are on the right and left eyes; and *dhaniṣṭhā* and *mūla* are on the right and left ears; then there are the eight beginning with *maghā*.

One should assign the constellations of the southern solstice to the curves of the left side; likewise, one should assign Mṛgaśīrṣa and the others of the northern solstice to the curves of the right side in reverse order. One should place Śatabhiṣā and Jyeṣṭhā on the right and left shoulders respectively.
Agastya is on the upper jaw, Yama on the lower jaw, Aṅgāraka (Mars) on the mouths, and Śanaiścara (Saturn).
Bṛhaspati is in the lap, Āditya on the crown of the head, Nārāyaṇa in the chest, Candra in the heart, Uśanas at the navel,

the Aśvins on the two breasts, Budha in the out-breath and in-breath, Rāhu in the throat, the Ketus in all the limbs, and all the hosts of stars in the body hairs. This, indeed, is the form of the Blessed Viṣṇu, consisting of all the deities, [to be meditated upon] at the daily junctions of day and night.

Being self-restrained and silent, gazing [upon it], he should worship with the words: "Obeisance to the world of light, to the one whose path is time, to the Lord of the unblinking [gods], to the Great Person; we offer our salutation.
This [world] consisting of planets, constellations, and stars is the transcendental aspect (ādhidaivika), which destroys the sins of those who recite mantras at the three junctions of the day.
For one who bows down to Him or remembers Him at the three junctions of the day, the sin committed during that time is quickly destroyed.
Śrī Śuka said:
Some say that ten thousand *yojanas* below the sun, Svarbhānu moves like a planet among the stars.
O dear one, that son of Siṃhikā, who was himself a wretch among the Asuras, yet obtained immortality and the status of a planet through the compassion of the Blessed One—
though he did not deserve it— we shall later describe his birth and deeds.
Furthermore, they say that this orb of the scorching sun extends for ten thousand yojanas in width.

Twelve thousand [yojanas] belong to Soma and thirteen thousand to Rāhu; that persistent enmity which, at the time of the lunar conjunction (parvan), causes obstruction as it rushes toward the sun and moon—
having heard of this, the Blessed One employed the weapon named Sudarśana for protection in both cases.
The *Bhāgavata* is his beloved weapon, unbearable due to its splendor as it revolves repeatedly;
standing before it for a moment, trembling and with a startled heart, one turns back from afar—this, people say, is its eclipse (*uparāga*).
Below that, at exactly that same distance, are the dwellings of the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Vidyādharas.
Below that is the playground of the hosts of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Pretas, and Bhūtas, extending as far as the atmosphere where the wind blows and where clouds are perceived.
Below that, at an interval of one hundred yojanas, is this earth, reaching down as far as the preeminent birds such as the Haṃsas, Bhāsas, Śyenās, and Suparṇas fly upward.
Thus has been described the configuration and location of the earth, even beneath the world of the waters.

The seven subterranean realms— Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, and Pātāla— are each fashioned with a length and breadth of ten thousand yojanas, separated from one another by the same distance (BhP 5.24.8).
Indeed, within these subterranean heavens, there are enjoyments of desire, sovereignty, bliss, prosperity, and splendor that exceed even those of heaven.

In their well-furnished palaces, gardens, pleasure groves, and dwellings, the Daityas, Dānavas, and Kādraveyas reside, enjoying themselves with the constant delight and affection of their wives, children, kinsmen, friends, and attendants.
As householders, their desires are unimpeded even by the Lord himself, and they find diversion in illusory magic.

O Great King, in those places dwell cities constructed by the master of illusion, Maya, featuring various wonderful mansions, walls, gate-towers, assembly halls, shrines, courtyards, sanctuaries, and other structures, all fashioned from the finest and most excellent jewels.
Adorned with artificial grounds filled with pairs of nāgas and asuras, pigeons, parrots, and mynah birds, and graced with the finest dwellings of the lords of the subterranean realms,
the gardens shine forth exceedingly, with trees whose beautiful branches are bent down by clusters of flowers, fruits, and lovely sprouts that delight the mind and the senses.

These [forests], where various birds dwell in pairs with their splendors embraced by the bodies of creepers; where the waters are filled with pure water and agitated by schools of leaping fish; and where dwellings are established amidst groves of lotuses, white lilies, blue water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, white esculent lilies, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and hundred-petaled roses—surpass the splendor of the world of the immortals with festivals for the senses consisting of sweet and diverse sounds that disturb the solitary wanderer.
In that place, indeed, no fear is perceived through the divisions of time such as day and night;
for there, the crest-jewels of the foremost great serpents dispel all darkness.
Nor does [fear] arise for those dwelling there from divine herbs, juices, elixirs, food, drink, bathing, and so forth.
Mental anxieties, physical ailments, wrinkles, graying hair, old age, and so forth, as well as discoloration of the body, foul odor, perspiration, fatigue, and exhaustion—
these are the stages of life;
yet for those auspicious ones, death does not prevail from any source whatsoever, except by the splendor of the Blessed One manifested through the Discus.
When he enters, the fetuses of the demonesses generally miscarry or fall out due to sheer fear.

Now, in Atala dwells the demon Bala, the son of Maya, by whom ninety-six illusions were created here, some of which even today the masters of illusion still maintain; and from the mouth of him as he yawns, three groups of women emerge.

There arose women who were wanton, lustful, and unchaste—those who, having enticed with passion a man who had entered their lairs by means of a substance called *hāṭaka*, would indeed sport with him at will through their own amorous glances, affectionate smiles, conversation, embraces, and so forth; and when that substance was consumed, a man would possess the strength of ten thousand great elephants, thinking, "I am a lord! I am a perfected one!"
Thinking highly of himself, he boasts like one blinded by intoxication (BhP 5.24.17).
Below that, at Vitala, is the blessed Lord Hara, Hāṭakeśvara, surrounded by his own attendants and hosts of spirits;
there Bhava dwells in union with Bhavānī for the sake of augmenting the creation of Prajāpati, from whom [this lineage] has proceeded.
By the power of you two, there is a preeminent river named Hāṭakī, where Citrabhānu, being kindled by Mātariśvan with vigor,
drinks that which is spat out; this gold known as hāṭaka is worn as an ornament by men together with women in the inner apartments of the lords of the Asuras.
Below that, in Sutala, is Bali, the son of Virocana, whose fame is exalted and whose glory is sacred.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to Mahendra, the Blessed Lord assumed a body born of Aditi in the form of a young dwarf (Vāmana);
having thus eclipsed the three worlds, he was restored to them again by the Lord’s very compassion—a grace not possessed by Indra and the other gods.
Endowed with abundant prosperity and honoring that very Lord who is worthy of worship through his own duty,
he now remains free from all fear.
This is not at all the direct result of the gift of land, for that [gift] belongs to the Lord alone among all classes of living beings.

The sovereignty of the cave-dwellers [the serpents] belongs to that which is offered with supreme faith and a mind composed by the highest reverence to Vāsudeva— the Supreme Self who has become the individual soul, the most excellent of holy places, and the worthy recipient— directly opening the door to liberation;
for even one who, being helpless during sneezing, falling, or stumbling, utters His name but once...
A person easily shakes off the bondage of karma for whom there is indeed this counteraction; however, those seeking liberation perceive it otherwise.
For all self-possessed devotees, He—the Giver of the Self—acts as the Self through His very nature as the Self.
Surely the Blessed Lord did not favor him, since He further extended the sovereignty of illusory enjoyments, which causes the loss of remembrance of the Self.

"Since that Lord, by means other than those previously employed— under the pretext of begging— has stripped me of my three worlds, leaving only my own body, and has now bound me with the nooses of Varuṇa and cast me into a mountain cave," he said,
"surely this Blessed One is not skilled in matters of statecraft, he who is the counselor of Indra."

Having been chosen exclusively for the office of mantra-maker, Bṛhaspati bypassed him and personally requested himself from Upendra, as well as blessings for himself; yet he did not at all accept that service. For one of such profound age, this triple world is but a mere moment within the revolution of a *manvantara* of Time, whose non-service even our grandfather Brahmā is said to have chosen over the supreme state of the Blessed One—which is free from fear on all sides—even though it was being offered by the Lord when [Brahmā] had ceased [his own duties].
Indeed, regarding his own father, [the sage thought]:
"Who else like me, whose impurities have not been cleansed and who has fallen away from the grace of the Lord, would wish to approach that high-souled one?
His life story will be related in detail later on; for the Blessed One himself, the teacher of the entire world, [was his guru].

Nārāyaṇa stands at the gate, mace in hand, his heart compassionate toward his own people— he by whom, with the big toe of his foot, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa was cast ten thousand times ten thousand yojanas away during the conquest of the quarters (BhP 5.24.28). Below that, in Talātala, is the lord of the Dānavas named Maya, the ruler of Tripura, who was [conquered] by the Blessed One.

Desiring the welfare of the three worlds, Mahādeva—the enemy of Tripura—burned his own three cities; by that Lord's grace, the preceptor of illusionists, having attained his station and being protected by Mahādeva, dwells in glory, free from the fear of the Sudarśana discus.
Below that, in Mahātala, resides Krodhavaśa, the lord of the many-headed serpents, the sons of Kadrū.

The group known as the Nāgas—headed by Kuhaka, Takṣaka, Kāliya, Suṣeṇa, and others—possessing great coils, constantly tremble before Puruṣavāha, the king of birds; yet, distracted by attachment to their wives, children, friends, and families, they sport here and there in negligence.
Below that, in the subterranean realm of Rasātala, dwell the Daityas, Dānavas, and those called Paṇis, as well as the Nivātakavacas.

The Kāleyas, inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura, who were enemies of the gods, possessed great power by birth and were exceedingly audacious; yet, their strength and arrogance having been struck down by the splendor of Lord Hari— the source of majesty for all the worlds— they dwell like creatures in a hole, terrified of Indra by the words of Saramā, the messenger of Indra, which were like the syllables of a mantra.

Below that, in the netherworld (pātāla), dwell the lords of the serpent realm (nāga-loka), headed by Vāsuki— namely Śaṅkha, Kulika, Mahāśaṅkha, Śveta, Dhanañjaya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhacūḍa, Kambala, Aśvatara, Devadatta, and others—
who possess great coils and are highly irascible. Indeed, upon the hoods of these beings, who have five, seven, ten, a hundred,
or a thousand heads, are arrayed magnificent, radiant jewels which dispel the mass of darkness within the caverns of Pātāla by their own luster.
Śrī Śuka said:

At a distance of thirty thousand yojanas from its base lies that which is known as the Tamasic potency (kalā) of the Blessed Lord, called Ananta by the Sātvatas; it is characterized by the egoistic conceit (*ahaṃkāra*) that effects the conjunction of the seer and the seen.
They call him Saṅkarṣaṇa,
of whose infinite-formed Lord, who possesses a thousand heads, this circle of the earth appears like a single mustard seed resting upon but one head; indeed,
when he desires to withdraw this world by means of Time, his beautiful, revolving eyebrows are knit with indignation.
In the meantime, a Rudra named Sāṅkarṣaṇa, the eleventh manifestation, rose up with three eyes, brandishing a trident with three prongs.
Upon the circles of the clusters of jewel-like nails, bright and ruddy upon his pair of lotus feet,
the lords of serpents bowed together with the best of the Sātvatas through the yoga of exclusive devotion, their cheeks adorned by the radiance of their shimmering earrings.

With hearts full of joy, they indeed gazed upon those most enchanting [limbs]; for the daughters of the Naga king, seeking his blessings, were anointing with pastes of agallochum, sandalwood, and saffron the silver pillars of his arms— which were beautiful, lovely, radiant, vast, white, and auspicious, adorned with the play of their graceful bracelets— and as they did so, their smiles were charming and playful, stirred by the onset of the fish-bannered god of love whose heart was agitated by the touch of him.
With his lotus-face and eyes casting compassionate glances, reddened and rolling from the intoxication of joy at her passion, he gazed at her with modesty;
that very Lord Ananta, an ocean of infinite virtues, the primordial God, having withdrawn the force of his indignation and wrath, remained for the welfare of the worlds,
being meditated upon by hosts of gods, asuras, serpents, siddhas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and sages.

With eyes agitated by the transformations of incessant joy and intoxication, being nourished by the nectar of Sulalitā’s sweet speech, he— clad in blue garments, wearing a single earring, and with his beautiful, auspicious arm resting upon the shoulder of the plow— became intoxicated by the honey-wine of the fragrance of fresh, unfading *tulasī* flowers; he beheld his own Vaijayantī forest garland, which possessed the splendor of the sweet songs of swarms of bees.
The Blessed One Mahendra, possessing noble grace, wears a golden girth like a lordly elephant.

He who is thus heard of, when meditated upon, quickly pierces the knot of the heart— composed of the qualities of goodness, passion, and darkness, woven by the impressions of karma from beginningless time and consisting of ignorance— which has entered within the heart of those seeking liberation.
By the power of that [Lord], the self-born Lord Nārada, together with Tumburu, praised Him in the assembly of Brahmā:
"The kalpas, which are the causes of this universe's origin, maintenance, and dissolution,
as well as the qualities of nature such as sattva and the rest, came into being by His glance alone."

How indeed can one know the path of that which is eternal, uncreated, and one, yet appears as manifold within the self? Out of great compassion, he has assumed a form for us— a manifestation of pure goodness (*sattva*).
In Him, who is the pure reality beyond both the existent and the non-existent, this entire universe shines forth;
it is He, of noble prowess, who assumed the blameless sport of the lion to win over the hearts of His own people.
If one should happen to recite His name—
whether out of distress, or if fallen, or even through negligence—
it instantly destroys all the sins of men, as well as those of others.
Upon what head of the Lord Śeṣa, who possesses a thousand heads, does the seeker of liberation rest like an atom— the entire terrestrial globe with its mountains, rivers, oceans, and living beings?
Who, even with a thousand tongues, could enumerate the heroic deeds of the Infinite One, whose prowess is immeasurable and who is the All-pervading Plenum?
Such is the power of the Blessed Lord Ananta.

Indeed, these are the very destinies to be attained here by men according to their karma, as described in accordance with the teachings for those desiring sense-objects. O King, I have thus explained, in response to your question, these various high and low, and dissimilar, results of the dharma characterized by worldly activity (pravṛtti). What else shall we tell you?
The King said:
"O great sage, how does this diversity of the world come about? The sage replied:
"Because the agent consists of the three *guṇas*, the various courses of action resulting from one's faith are all distinct for every person, according to their relative degrees."

Now, therefore, regarding unrighteousness (*adharma*) characterized by what is prohibited, the fruit of the action becomes dissimilar for the performer due to the very same lack of uniformity in their faith. Indeed, by means of beginningless ignorance, thousands of paths have proceeded as the manifestations of those performed desires; we shall describe them in detail according to their prevalence.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, what are these so-called hells? Are they specific regions, or are they outside the three worlds, or perhaps within them?
The Sage replied:

In the intermediate region of the three worlds, specifically in the southern direction, below the earth and above the waters, dwell the hosts of ancestors (pitṛs) such as the Agniṣvāttas; in that quarter, they reside with supreme concentration, offering truly effective blessings for their own lineages.

Indeed, in that realm where the Blessed Lord Vaivasvata, the King of the Ancestors, having brought deceased beings to his own domain by means of his servants according to their respective karmic faults, exercises punishment along with his attendants— never transgressing the command of the Blessed Lord.

In that regard, some enumerate twenty-one hells; O King, we shall now describe them to you in order according to their names, forms, and characteristics: Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Raurava, Maharaurava, Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, Asipatravana, Sūkaramukha, Andhakūpa, Kṛmibhojana, Sandaṃśa, Taptasūrmi, Vajrakaṇṭaka-śālmalī, and Vaitaraṇī.
Pūyoda, Prāṇarodha, Viśasana, Lālābhakṣa, Sārameyādana, Avīci, Ayaḥpāna, as well as Kṣārakardama, Rakṣogaṇabhojana, Śūlaprota, Dandaśūka, Avaṭanirodhana, Paryāvartana,
and Sūcīmukha— these are the twenty-eight hells, which are the sites of various forms of torment.

In that regard, he who seizes the wealth, children, or wife of another is indeed bound by the noose of Time; seized by the most terrifying messengers of Yama, he is forcibly cast into the Tāmisra hell. There, being tormented by agonies such as starvation, lack of water, flogging with rods, and threats, the creature—having reached a state of utter dejection—falls into a swoon all at once in that place which is almost entirely Tāmisra.
In this very way, in the hell Andhatāmisra, he who deceives a person and enjoys his wife and other possessions—
there, as the embodied soul is cast down and stands in torment, his intellect is destroyed and his vision is lost,
like a tree whose roots are being severed; therefore, they designate that place as Andhatāmisra.

But he who, thinking "I am this" or "this is mine," nourishes only his own family day after day by harming living beings— he, having abandoned them here, falls himself by their inauspiciousness into the Raurava hell.
And those living beings who were harmed here by him in the same manner as they were, undergo the torments of Yama in the next world.
Those very same beings, having become *ruru* deer, likewise injure that person; therefore, it is called *Raurava*. *Ruru* is a designation for a creature even more cruel than a serpent.
In the same way is *Mahāraurava*, where the *ruru* deer named *kravyāda* ("flesh-eaters") cause the fallen person—who is merely a nourisher of his own body—to be killed by their own flesh.

But he who here, being fierce, roasts living beings— be they cattle or birds— while they are breathing, that merciless man, despised even by cannibals, is roasted in boiling oil in the Kumbhīpāka hell by the attendants of Yama in the next world. And he who here is a betrayer of the brāhmaṇas falls into the hell named Kālasūtra, which is ten thousand yojanas in circumference.

He remains, sits, moves about, stands, and runs upon a heated copper frying pan, being intensely scorched from above by fire and from below by the sun, while his inner and outer bodies are consumed by hunger and thirst; he stays there for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the body of a beast.

But him who, in this world, has departed from the path of his own Veda without being in distress and has instead resorted to heresy, they cast into the Forest of Sword-Leaves; there, as he runs hither and thither, they strike him with whips, and while all his limbs are being cut by the sharp-edged sword-leaves of the palm forest, he cries out with supreme agony, "Alas! I am slain!"

Fainting at every step, the violator of his own dharma falls and reaps the fruit of following heretical paths. But that king or royal official who inflicts punishment upon one who is exempt from punishment, or corporal punishment upon a brāhmaṇa, becomes most sinful and falls in the next world into the Sūkaramukha hell; there, his limbs are crushed by those of exceeding strength.

Just as a stalk of sugarcane here, crying out with a piteous sound, might somewhere faint and fall into a state of exhaustion; even so, those whose faults are unseen are obstructed [by their own actions]. But he who, while his own livelihood is provided by the Lord for beings whose subsistence is ordained by Him and who do not discern the suffering of others, yet—having himself fashioned his own livelihood—inflicts pain upon them who are sensitive to the suffering of others, he falls into the blind well in the next world.

By virtue of having oppressed those beings, he falls there; pursued on all sides by those creatures— beasts, deer, birds, reptiles, mosquitoes, lice, bedbugs, flies, and whatever others he had oppressed— he wanders about in darkness, his sleep and comfort destroyed, finding no place of rest,
just as a soul in a diseased body.

But he who, without sharing here whatever has been obtained, eats while failing to perform the five sacrifices, is praised as a crow; he falls in the next world into the lowest hell called Kṛmibhojana. There, in a pit of worms extending for hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, having himself become a worm, being devoured by other worms, he remains a "worm-eater" as long as that state of eating what has not been given or offered persists.
"One who torments himself through penance [attains liberation].
But that man here, O King, who— whether by theft or by force— seizes gold, jewels, and other valuables belonging to a Brāhmaṇa or anyone else when there is no emergency,
him the servants of Yama in the next world flay with iron balls and tongs upon his skin."
But he who here approaches a woman who should not be approached, or a woman who approaches a man who should not be approached—
therein they strike them with whips and cause the man to embrace a red-hot iron female image, and the woman to embrace a male iron image.
But those who in this world indeed practice all forms of illicit conduct, them they drag out after placing them upon the *vajra-kaṇṭaka-śālmalī* tree while they remain in hell.

And those kṣatriyas or royal officials in this world who, being heretics, break the bridges of dharma— they, having passed away with their boundaries of conduct shattered, fall into the Vaitaraṇī river, which serves as a moat for that hell.
In that river, being devoured here and there by swarms of aquatic creatures, yet not being separated from their own lives as they are carried along,
they suffer in torment within the stream flowing with feces, urine, pus, blood, hair, nails, bones, fat, flesh, and marrow, while recollecting the ripening of their own evil karma—
those who, in this world, were husbands of low-caste women (*vṛṣalī*), having lost their purity, conduct, and observances, and abandoned all shame.

Those who practice the conduct of beasts also fall, after death, into an ocean filled with pus, feces, urine, phlegm, and filth, where they eat that which is most loathsome. Furthermore, those Brahmins and others who, being masters of dogs and donkeys, sport in hunting and kill deer even at improper places—when they have passed away, the messengers of Yama make them targets... [and strike them].
Those who,

being hypocrites here, slaughter animals in sacrifices performed for ostentation— the lords of hell torture them after they have fallen into the Vaiśasa hell and then slaughter them. Furthermore, that twice-born man who, deluded by lust, makes his wife of equal caste drink his semen, the doer of evil is cast into a river of semen in the next world and made to drink it.
But those who are indeed robbers here— those who set fires,

those who administer poison, or those kings and royal soldiers who plunder villages or caravans— even they, having passed away, are impetuously devoured by seven hundred and twenty dogs with adamantine fangs, the messengers of Yama.

But he who here speaks untruth in testimony, in the exchange of goods, or in giving, by whatever means, indeed, after death, is cast headlong from the summit of a mountain a hundred yojanas high into the bottomless hell Avīci, which lacks any space; there, where the surface of stone appears like water, his body is shattered into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
One who is dying does not fall back once he has been mounted [upon the funeral pyre].
However, if a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya here who is a drinker of Soma, or his wife,
or one observing a vow, should drink liquor even through negligence, then having led them to hell, [the deity] shall step upon their chests with his foot and [drink] from their mouths.
Just as they pour molten black iron into fire, so too,

he who here, out of self-conceit, does not highly regard one who is superior by virtue of birth, austerity, knowledge, conduct, caste, or stage of life, is indeed already dead; having died, he falls headlong into the hell of alkaline mire.

For those men here who sacrifice with the human sacrifice (puruṣamedha), and those women who devour human victims as if they were beasts— once slain, they endure endless torments in the abode of Yama, being made to suffer by hosts of Rākṣasas like butchers.
Having cut out flesh with their knives, they drink the blood; dancing and singing, they rejoice just like man-eaters here in this world (BhP 5.26.31).

Moreover, those who here in the forest or in the village—by means of deceptive devices—cause innocent people who trust them to settle down, and then, while they still desire to live, pierce them onto spikes, strings, and the like for the sake of sport, they too, after death, undergo the torments of Yama.
Those whose souls are impaled upon stakes and the like, who are afflicted by hunger and thirst, and who are struck here and there by sharp-beaked herons, vultures, and other birds,
remember their own past sins (BhP 5.26.32).
But those men of fierce nature who, in this world, cause terror to living beings, just as venomous serpents do;
They too, after death, fall into the hell called Dandaśūka, O King, where five-faced and seven-faced venomous serpents approach and swallow them as if they were creatures living in holes;
and those who here on earth confine living beings in blind pits, granaries, caves, and the like, are likewise confined there in those very places and suffocated with smoke by a fire of pitch.

Moreover, if a householder here repeatedly looks upon guests or visitors with an evil eye, his anger having been aroused as if he wished to burn them, then in hell, vultures, herons, crows, cranes, and other birds with diamond-hard beaks will forcibly pluck out the eyes of that man of sinful vision by their great strength.
But he who, whether here or there, possesses the conceit of wealth and egoism, looking askance, suspicious of everything,

his heart and face withered by anxiety over the expenditure and loss of riches— he, like a demon, guards his wealth without finding peace; and after death, having been seized by the impurity of producing, increasing, and protecting that wealth, he enters the needle-mouthed hell.

The messengers of Dharmarāja cast that sinful man, who has seized the wealth of others, into hell; there, like weavers, they wind him all over his limbs with cords. There are hundreds and thousands of such hells in the abode of Yama, and in all of them—
O Lord of the Earth, all those who follow unrighteousness—whether mentioned here or not—enter into that [state] by turns;

likewise, those who follow righteousness enter into the other. But here, in this world of rebirth, they enter by means of the remnants of both. The path characterized by cessation (nivṛtti) has already been explained at the very beginning; such indeed is the extent of the cosmic egg (aṇḍakośa).

That which is described in the Purāṇas as being divided into fourteen types is the most massive form of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, composed of the qualities of His own *māyā*. He who respectfully recites, hears, or causes others to hear this description—
his intellect purified by faith and devotion— knows that ungraspable form of the Blessed Supreme Self, even though it is beyond the reach of the senses.

"Having heard that the ascetic should first bring his self under control through the gross form of the Lord and then gradually lead it to the subtle form by means of the intellect," [he describes] the earth,
islands, regions, rivers, mountains, sky, and oceans—
O King, I have described to you the arrangement of the netherworlds, the directions, the hells, and the celestial spheres; and I have sung of the wonderful,
gross body of the Lord, which is the abode of all classes of living beings.
